Huawei today held its autumn product launch event in Shanghai, unveiling the Mate 90 series. The series includes five models: the Mate 90, Mate 90 Pro, Mate 90 Pro Max, Mate 90 Pro Max Collector’s Edition, and Mate 90 RS Ultimate Design. Prices range from RMB 5,999 ($895) to RMB 12,999 ($1,939).

The main upgrades in the Mate 90 series focus on the chip, display, camera system, connectivity, and on-device AI. The new generation of Kirin chips across the lineup was one of the key highlights of the launch.

New-generation Kirin chips across the lineup

The Mate 90 is powered by the Kirin 9030. According to Huawei, its overall performance is 27% higher than that of the previous-generation Mate 80.

The Mate 90 Pro uses the Kirin 9035, which Huawei says focuses on balancing performance and power consumption. Its overall battery life has improved by 18% compared with the previous generation, according to the company.

The higher-end Mate 90 Pro Max and above are powered by the Kirin 9050 Pro. According to Huawei, the chip uses a new logical folding architecture with 5 million signal transmission bonds and achieves an inter-die bandwidth of 125 TB per second. Huawei says overall device performance is 31% higher than the previous generation, while on-device AI computing performance has doubled.

The different Kirin chips allow Huawei to maintain performance differences between the various Mate 90 models.

Display and device protection

On the display side, the Mate 90 Pro and higher-end models feature second-generation Linglong displays, with peak brightness reaching up to 12,000 nits at 1% APL.

The Mate 90 Pro Max and RS Ultimate Design further feature full-color Linglong displays with support for BT.2020 full-chain color reproduction. For general users, this mainly relates to brightness and color performance, while content creators gain additional display capabilities aimed at more professional use.

For device protection, the entire lineup uses third-generation Xuanwu strengthened Kunlun Glass, while the Pro and higher-end models use optical Kunlun Glass for the camera cover. Huawei says the overall drop resistance of the devices has improved by 20 times compared with the previous generation.

All models also support IP68 dust and water resistance, while the Pro and higher-end models add IP69 protection against high-temperature, high-pressure water jets.

Camera upgrades focus on color, dynamic range and telephoto

For imaging, the entire Mate 90 series features a third-generation Red Maple primary-color camera system and infrared optical coatings across the full focal range. Huawei says global color accuracy has improved by 37%, while skin-tone reproduction accuracy in portrait photography has improved by 62%.

The Mate 90 Pro Max takes the camera system further with an 18-stop high-dynamic-range main camera and a 200-megapixel large-sensor telephoto camera. Its stabilization is rated at CIPA 7.5. Huawei says the system has been further optimized for image stability and clarity at 20x zoom, while also improving noise control in low-light conditions.

These upgrades target several areas that have become key points of competition in smartphone imaging, including color reproduction, dynamic range, telephoto performance, and image stabilization.

On-device AI becomes another focus

For connectivity, the Mate 90 series uses a Wi-Fi and cellular integrated antenna architecture. Huawei says the design can increase signal strength by 2 dB and improve connection stability in complex environments. The Mate 90 Pro Max also supports four SIM cards with three active simultaneously.

On the AI side, the Mate 90 Pro Max and higher-end models feature a 30-billion-parameter MoE multimodal on-device model, along with functions such as Xiaoyi Call 2.0, Xiaoyi Gallery Assistant, and Xiaoyi Navigation Bar.

Compared with AI services that rely primarily on cloud computing, on-device models allow some tasks to be processed directly on the smartphone without requiring a continuous network connection. However, the actual experience will depend on the capabilities of individual models, response times, and specific usage scenarios.

The move toward larger on-device models

The Mate 90 series continues Huawei’s multi-model strategy, using differences in chips, displays, and camera systems to cover a range of price segments.

Compared with simply adding hardware specifications, a more notable change in this generation is the combination of the new chips with on-device AI. As large language models increasingly move onto smartphones, phone makers are shifting from simply offering AI-powered applications toward deploying larger models directly on devices.

Whether these hardware and AI upgrades translate into meaningful improvements in everyday use will ultimately depend on hands-on experience and longer-term testing.

]]> 199178 The Man Who Built China’s Screen Giant Is Betting on RISC-V https://technode.com/2026/09/30/the-man-who-built-chinas-screen-giant-is-betting-on-risc-v/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 03:16:13 +0000 https://technode.com/?p=199166 Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication. Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication.

Wang Dongsheng has already spent one career proving that a Chinese company could compete in one of the technology industry’s most capital-intensive businesses.

In 1993, he led the creation of BOE, the display manufacturer that would grow into one of the world’s largest producers of screens. BOE supplied the panels through which hundreds of millions of people encountered televisions, laptops and smartphones—even when they never saw its name.

Wang left the company’s chairmanship in 2019. At 62, an age when many founders would have stepped away from industrial risk, he started again.

His second act is ESWIN Computing, a Beijing chip company organized around RISC-V, the open instruction-set architecture attracting developers across embedded devices, automobiles, robotics and artificial intelligence. ESWIN is now preparing to list in Hong Kong, offering 1.57 billion H shares at between HK$1.48 and HK$1.59 each. Trading is expected to begin on October 9 under stock code 1256, according to its prospectus.

The comparison with BOE is tempting. Both companies emerged from moments when Chinese manufacturers wanted more control over a foundational layer of the electronics industry. Both required large, sustained investment before scale could improve their economics. Both were shaped by Wang’s belief that an industrial platform matters more than a single product.

But ESWIN is not yet the BOE of RISC-V. Most of its revenue still comes from chips that manage displays and touch interactions. It remains heavily lossmaking, depends on a small group of customers and is attempting to expand into several difficult markets at once.

That tension makes the company more interesting than its listing labels suggest. ESWIN’s Hong Kong offering is not simply a bet on an open chip architecture. It is a test of whether expertise accumulated around screens can become the foundation for a broader computing business—and whether Wang can repeat the logic of his first industrial transformation in a much less forgiving market.

The Industrialist Behind the Screen

To understand ESWIN, it helps to understand what Wang built before it.

BOE was founded in Beijing in 1993, when China’s electronics industry remained dependent on imported display technology and manufacturing equipment. Wang served as chairman and chief executive from the company’s creation until 2016, then remained chairman until his term ended in June 2019.

Display manufacturing is a business of scale, precision and punishing capital expenditure. A new production line can cost billions of dollars. Technical generations turn over quickly, and the value of a panel tends to decline as manufacturing improves. Competitors must finance the next factory before the previous one has fully paid for itself.

BOE survived that cycle and became a global display supplier. The experience appears to have shaped Wang’s view of technology companies: individual components matter, but the deeper objective is to assemble talent, intellectual property, manufacturing relationships and customers into a platform capable of surviving several product generations.

ESWIN Group was created in 2019 around that platform idea. Its semiconductor activities were separated into businesses covering chip products, 12-inch silicon wafers, board-level packaging and testing, and display-driver packaging and testing. ESWIN Computing took the chip-product business that had begun operating under a predecessor organization in 2018.

This distinction is important. ESWIN Computing does not manufacture wafers or package every chip it sells. It operates largely as a fabless company: it researches and designs chips, chipsets and circuit boards, develops the software required to use them, and relies on third parties for fabrication, packaging and testing.

The company was formally established in Beijing in September 2019. It also created a central research institute to work on RISC-V computing architecture, high-speed interfaces and reusable intellectual-property modules. Wang initially served as chairman. Mi Peng, who joined as chief financial officer in 2019, is now chairman and chief executive, while Wang remains an executive director and chairs the strategy and investment committee.

Other senior figures point to the kind of organization ESWIN wanted to build. Vice chairman Wang Bo spent almost 24 years at Intel, most recently as a product director. The broader technical team includes veterans of chip design, displays, connectivity and computing.

Rather than begin with one flagship processor, ESWIN accumulated a library. As of March 2026, it reported more than 620 IP modules, over 20 series of RISC-V cores and more than 1,740 patent applications incorporated across its products. It had commercialized over 150 hardware-software products and served 220 customers during the reporting period covered by its prospectus.

This breadth is both the company’s proposition and its first complication.

What RISC-V Actually Opens

RISC-V—pronounced “risk five”—is not a chip. It is an instruction-set architecture, or ISA: the basic vocabulary and rules that allow software to tell a processor what to do.

For decades, most personal computers and data-center processors have been built around the x86 instruction sets associated with Intel and AMD, while smartphones and countless embedded devices rely on architectures licensed from Arm. Chip designers can build their own processors around those systems, but they operate within commercially controlled ecosystems.

RISC-V is an open, royalty-free standard. Its core specifications can be used by companies, universities and developers to design processors without paying for the instruction set itself. The architecture is modular, allowing designers to begin with a relatively small base and add capabilities required for a specific product.

Open does not mean that every RISC-V chip must be open source. A company can use the public instruction set while keeping its processor design, specialized modules and software proprietary. The value of the standard is that it gives designers more freedom to customize hardware without abandoning a common software target.

That makes RISC-V particularly attractive for devices that sit outside the conventional PC and smartphone categories. A car controller, industrial sensor, storage appliance or robot may need a different balance of performance, power consumption, cost and real-time responsiveness. Developers can tailor a processor around those needs while reusing tools and software developed across the wider RISC-V ecosystem.

The difficult part is everything beyond the specification. A commercially useful chip needs verified processor cores, interfaces, compilers, operating systems, development tools, application software, documentation and engineers who can help customers integrate it. An architecture becomes powerful only when enough of that surrounding ecosystem exists.

ESWIN is trying to occupy the layer between the open standard and the finished device. It develops RISC-V cores and reusable IP, combines them with other processing and connectivity functions, packages those elements into chips or boards, and supplies the software required to make them work in particular applications.

The company calls its development environment RISAA. The platform is designed to let teams reuse hardware and software modules rather than begin each product from zero. ESWIN can sell finished products, customize them for major customers or license individual IP blocks to companies developing their own chips.

In theory, this creates a compounding advantage. Each project adds technology that can be reused in the next one, reducing development time and spreading research costs across a larger range of products. In practice, the benefits arrive only if enough customers choose the platform—and if the company can prevent its product range from becoming an expensive collection of unrelated projects.

The Display Business Paying for the Future

Despite its RISC-V positioning, ESWIN’s present business remains closely connected to Wang’s previous industry.

The company’s largest product group consists of human-machine interaction chips. These components sit inside televisions, monitors, laptops, smartphones and watches. Timing controllers organize the flow of image data toward a display. Touch controllers translate a finger’s movement into commands. Other chips manage power or help display drivers turn electronic signals into visible pixels.

These are rarely the parts advertised to consumers, but a screen cannot function without them. The display supply chain also gave ESWIN a ready set of engineering problems and customer relationships. In 2025, the company was China’s largest domestic provider of human-machine interaction chips for smart devices by revenue, according to market research commissioned for the prospectus.

Human-machine interaction products generated RMB1.86 billion in 2025, or 76.3% of ESWIN’s total revenue. Multimedia-processing chips—including television system-on-chips, monitor scalers and Mini-LED or Micro-LED controllers—added another 6.2%.

Together, screen-related products accounted for more than four-fifths of the business. They are not a historical footnote. They are the revenue base supporting ESWIN’s expansion.

The company has continued to develop that base. In 2025, a leading monitor manufacturer began mass production of a RISC-V multimedia controller supplied by ESWIN. Its OLED display-driver chip was adopted by a leading smartphone manufacturer. These products show how RISC-V can be introduced inside familiar devices, often in control functions invisible to the user.

They also reveal the limit of describing ESWIN as a computing startup. Its commercial strength was built around displays, an industry in which Wang already understood the technology, customers and supply chain. The more ambitious parts of the story are newer.

From Screens to Machines That Act

ESWIN divides its growth products into interconnectivity and computing.

Interconnectivity products allow vehicles, robots and industrial equipment to transmit and receive data through Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular networks. Computing products range from microcontrollers that manage a limited set of operations to AI systems-on-chips capable of processing sensor data and making decisions locally.

The company groups these markets under “embodied intelligence,” an industry term for machines that sense and act in the physical world. In practical terms, this includes cars coordinating electronic systems, robots interpreting their surroundings and industrial equipment responding to real-time conditions.

ESWIN began emphasizing edge and automotive products in 2021. It delivered its first 32-bit RISC-V IP that year and a 64-bit version in 2023. Its automotive development program followed in 2022. By 2025, a RISC-V microcontroller had entered mass production with an automotive-parts supplier and a vehicle manufacturer.

The company has moved further into computing through boards and systems. Its products now span edge-computing chips, multi-purpose computing hardware and video-transcoding cards. In 2026, it began developing a high-performance RISC-V AI system-on-chip for large-model inference. Another RISC-V AI chip was adopted by a consumer-storage manufacturer for personal-storage products.

The financial statements suggest that this activity is beginning to matter. Computing products generated only RMB375,000 in 2023. Revenue rose to RMB72.3 million in 2024 and RMB319.8 million in 2025, reaching 13.2% of the company total.

During the first three months of 2026, computing revenue reached RMB223 million, almost half of quarterly sales. That number should be treated carefully: large system projects can make one quarter look very different from the next. It nevertheless shows why ESWIN wants investors to view it as more than a display-chip supplier.

The transition is not a conventional pivot. ESWIN has not abandoned screens to chase AI. It is attempting to reuse the same platform—processor cores, interfaces, software and supply-chain relationships—across devices that require more connectivity and local computing.

The question is whether that reuse is technically and economically real. A timing controller for a monitor, an automotive microcontroller and an inference chip operate under very different requirements. Shared architecture can lower part of the development burden, but every market still demands specialized engineering, qualification and customer support.

The Cost of Building Before Scale

ESWIN’s revenue has grown steadily. It rose from RMB1.75 billion in 2023 to RMB2.03 billion in 2024 and RMB2.43 billion in 2025. Gross margin improved from 15.4% to 18.6% over the same period.

The company remains far from profitable.

ESWIN lost RMB1.84 billion in 2023, RMB1.55 billion in 2024 and RMB1.52 billion in 2025. It lost a further RMB374.9 million during the first quarter of 2026 and says it expects losses to continue for the foreseeable future.

Research and development explains much of the gap. R&D expense reached RMB1.44 billion in 2023—more than 80% of revenue that year—and remained above RMB1 billion in 2025. Administrative and sales expenses add another layer of cost, while new products require investment long before they produce meaningful volume.

This is where comparisons with BOE become useful and dangerous at the same time. Both displays and chips reward patient investment, but they scale differently. A panel factory can produce large volumes of relatively standardized output once capacity is installed. A chip-platform company must repeatedly persuade customers to design its technology into products, then maintain software and engineering support across many applications.

ESWIN argues that reuse will gradually improve the economics. Once a processor core, interface or software module has been developed and verified, it can be incorporated into several products. Higher shipment volumes can spread tape-out, software and support costs across more units. Customized projects can also create reusable modules for later customers.

There are signs of improvement. Adjusted net loss narrowed from RMB1.70 billion in 2023 to RMB1.16 billion in 2025, after excluding share-based payments and listing expenses. Gross profit rose each year. But ESWIN is still spending ahead of the scale required to support its platform.

The Hong Kong offering will extend that runway. At the midpoint of its price range, the company expects approximately HK$2.27 billion in net proceeds. It plans to allocate 35% to developing and updating chip products, 30% to the RISAA hardware-software platform, 15% to potential acquisitions, 10% to marketing and the RISC-V ecosystem, and 10% to working capital.

That allocation makes the purpose of the listing unusually clear: investors are being asked to finance more platform before the existing platform has reached profitability.

The Customer Behind the Concentration

ESWIN’s revenue base is not only concentrated by product. It is concentrated by customer.

The five largest customers generated 89.5% of revenue in 2025. The largest alone contributed 64.6%, although that was down from 82.1% in 2023. During the first quarter of 2026, the largest customer’s share fell to 39.3% as computing revenue expanded.

Such concentration is common when a young chip supplier wins a high-volume design with a major electronics manufacturer. It can accelerate growth because one successful product reaches millions of devices. It also gives the customer significant influence over pricing, inventory and the timing of orders.

ESWIN’s prospectus does not identify its largest customer by name. It describes the company as a Shenzhen-listed provider of intelligent interface products and professional services that buys mainly human-machine interaction chips for televisions, monitors and smartphones.

The relationship places ESWIN’s BOE heritage in the background even when the customer remains anonymous. Wang’s industry experience made it possible to begin with a market the company understood. The long-term test is whether ESWIN can build a customer base that no longer depends so heavily on any one display ecosystem.

Inventory creates a related risk. Net inventory rose from RMB328.6 million at the end of 2023 to RMB780.1 million by March 2026 as the company prepared for new products and anticipated demand. Earlier-generation connectivity products had already required substantial write-downs. In chips, preparing too little inventory can mean missing a customer launch; preparing too much can leave expensive components obsolete.

The platform strategy is meant to diversify both products and customers. It will succeed only if the newer automotive, robotics, industrial and computing products move from technical milestones into repeatable sales.

A Second Industrial Bet

Wang Dongsheng’s first major company helped shift the geography of display manufacturing. ESWIN is attempting something less visible and potentially broader: building reusable computing technology that can appear inside many categories of machines.

RISC-V gives the company an opening. The architecture lowers one barrier to processor design and offers customers an alternative to proprietary instruction sets. It does not remove the harder barriers—software, verification, manufacturing, customer trust and the enormous cost of sustaining a product roadmap.

ESWIN has assembled many of the necessary pieces. It has commercial products, large customers, processor cores, a growing IP library and a founder who has already endured one long industrial cycle. Its display business provides revenue and a route into high-volume devices. Its computing products are beginning to change the mix.

It also has the profile of a company still proving the central claim behind its existence. Revenue remains dominated by screen-related chips. Losses remain large. Customer concentration remains high. AI inference, robotics and automotive computing are promising markets, but they are also crowded with established chipmakers and heavily funded startups.

The Hong Kong listing does not resolve those contradictions. It gives ESWIN more time and capital to work through them.

That may be the most revealing connection between Wang’s two companies. BOE was not built through a single technological breakthrough; it was built through repeated investment, manufacturing discipline and the willingness to remain in a difficult industry long enough for scale to matter.

ESWIN is now making a similar argument about computing platforms. The difference is that an open architecture allows many companies to start. Only a few will build enough technology around it to make customers stay.

According to sources, the project began internal testing as early as April and was previously known internally as Spell. ByteDance’s AI assistant Doubao is reportedly accelerating work on a new personal AI agent. According to sources, the project began internal testing as early as April and was previously known internally as Spell. Product development has recently picked up pace, with a public launch expected in the near future.

The move could mark a shift in Doubao’s evolution from an AI chatbot toward a more autonomous agent that can handle tasks on behalf of users, rather than simply responding to prompts.

Internally tested since April, initially developed by the Doubao Phone Assistant team

According to Sina Tech, Spell was initially led by the Doubao Phone Assistant team and entered small-scale internal testing in April. The core idea was to move AI beyond simply answering questions and toward actually completing tasks on behalf of users, an approach increasingly described in the industry as a Personal Agent.

The project had not previously been disclosed publicly. One factor was the development timeline of Doubao’s phone assistant, while the broader concept of personal AI agents was still at a relatively early stage.

That appears to be changing. As products such as Meta Muse and OpenAI’s “o” have attracted growing attention overseas, Personal Agents are moving from an emerging concept toward a product category that major AI companies are increasingly competing in. This has also prompted Doubao to accelerate development of its own personal AI agent.

Spell’s technology is now being folded into Doubao

The new product is not being built entirely from scratch. Sources said Doubao is now integrating the technical capabilities developed through the original Spell project with core capabilities from the Doubao conversational AI team. The two teams are expected to jointly work on further product development and launch.

Looking at the bigger picture, the project can be seen as an extension of Doubao’s technical work on mobile AI agents over the past two years.

In December 2025, Doubao first unveiled a technical preview of its phone assistant. A consumer version followed in September this year. After multiple rounds of validation in mobile scenarios, Doubao is now looking to extend those agent capabilities from a phone assistant into a more general-purpose personal assistant.

The phone assistant may have been just the starting point. Personal Agent could be the next direction Doubao is exploring.

Doubao is building out its agent portfolio

Doubao has already been expanding its presence in the Agent space. On August 25, it launched Doubao Work, an Agent product designed for enterprise and office scenarios. It can handle tasks ranging from drafting documents and organizing meeting notes to processing data across different software tools.

The company has since added features including editing of local Office files, task handoffs across up to five devices, and the ability to create customized skills through screen recordings.

The overall direction is becoming increasingly clear: for businesses, AI can help you get work done. For consumers, it could help manage everyday tasks and personal affairs. If the personal AI agent launches as expected, Doubao would effectively be pursuing two parallel agent tracks: enterprise applications and consumer use.

AI agents are moving from chatting to doing

Over the past two years, AI competition has largely focused on model capabilities, reasoning and generation quality. But as AI agents evolve, the focus is shifting from answering questions to getting things done.

Users increasingly want AI that can remember preferences, understand goals and complete tasks on their behalf, from gathering information and handling software to organizing content and executing workflows.

That is where Doubao’s potential personal assistant fits in. Rather than simply adding another chatbot, it could extend Doubao’s existing agent capabilities into a broader personal AI assistant for everyday use. How far it can go, however, will only become clear after the product launches.

Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

On Sept. 23, SenseTime launched SenseMart OS at its Shanghai headquarters, positioning it as a physical operating system for retail. The system connects heterogeneous robots, retail equipment, and commercial operations, offering operators, brands, and venues a deployable, operable, and replicable embodied-retail solution. At the event, the SenseMart Go robotic store demonstrated how the OS can coordinate these components in a real-world retail setting.

Why it matters: SenseMart OS offers a glimpse of how embodied intelligence could move beyond demonstrations and into everyday commercial environments.

  • The launch also reflects a broader debate over what will define the next phase of competition in embodied intelligence: robot hardware, data, models, or systems?

Why retail: SenseTime already had years of experience in the sector, with product-recognition systems processing millions of orders daily and a database covering more than 300,000 SKUs, or distinct product types and variants, Dr. Yi Shuai, co-founder and chief scientist of SenseTime Smart Retail, told TechNode.

  • Unlike warehouses or factories, retail requires robots to interact with people, testing perception, interaction, decision-making, and execution at the same time.
  • Retail also offers clear business metrics, such as sales, repeat purchases, and ROI, that can be used to evaluate whether the technology is working.

Zoom in: Dr. Yi said SenseMart OS focuses on three elements that support four core capabilities — perception, interaction, decision-making, and execution — as SenseTime looks to expand the system beyond retail into other offline service industries.

Business outcomes: The system targets metrics such as customer satisfaction, repeat purchases, and transaction completion, not just robot task success.

Multiple robot types: It can connect wheeled dual-arm robots, humanoids, grippers, and other hardware depending on the task.

  • Retail data: It combines visual, transaction, inventory, and voice-interaction data across the customer journey to train retail agents.

By the numbers:

  • One employee can currently support three to five stores, cutting average staffing to about 0.2–0.3 workers per location, Dr. Yi says.
  • The robots can run for about six hours on a charge and typically need charging twice a day. If a customer arrives while one is charging, it can leave the dock to serve them first.
  • Strong Shanghai locations can reportedly break even in about six to 12 months; average sites take around a year.
  • Each store carries about 150–200 SKUs, roughly one-third to one-fifth the assortment of a small convenience store.

The scaling play:

  • SenseMart OS can learn one new equipment-handling skill per week at a store and replicate it across existing and future locations.
  • Training a new store model has fallen from two to three months at the first location to about one to two weeks today.
  • Standardized deployments can begin operating the day after installation, according to Dr. Yi.

On the ground: SenseMart Go now operates more than 20 stores across cities including Shanghai, Hefei, Shenzhen, Qingdao, and Yancheng, spanning campuses, malls, offices, industrial parks, events, and public spaces.

What to watch: Speakers at the event pointed to different areas where the next wave of value in embodied intelligence could emerge.

  • Industry know-how: “The industry’s greatest value will move toward both ends — upstream supply chains and downstream industry data and expertise,” Dr. Yi said. SenseTime Smart Retail is focusing on the latter through retail.
  • Systems: “What matters more is getting embodied intelligence into production and daily life than the system or foundation model itself,” said Weisheng Xu, co-founder and CEO of Jiutian Yuanshu. For now, systems can help bridge gaps between foundation models and real-world deployment.
  • Real-world data: “Every time a robot works in a real-world setting, the flywheel of models and data turns once,” said Min Yuheng, co-founder and CEO of Zerith Robotics. Real deployments, he argued, are key to improving both data and models.

Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

When photovoltaic panels develop defects such as hot spots, physical damage, dust buildup, or other obstructions, workers have traditionally had to inspect them one by one, often at height. The process is time-consuming, physically demanding, and potentially dangerous, while also increasing maintenance costs and safety risks.

What if drones and robots could work together?

The result is a form of low-altitude intelligence that can support both inspection and maintenance.

This is more than a futuristic concept. Companies around the world are already exploring this kind of drone-robot collaboration. Skysys Intelligent Technology is part of broader industry efforts to bring drones and robots together for inspection and maintenance.

According to company data, its systems have been deployed at more than 1,400 renewable-energy sites worldwide, covering over 40 GW of installed capacity.

The company raised more than RMB 100 million in a Series B+ round in June 2025, following a similarly sized Series B a year earlier. The latest funding would go toward productizing its renewable-energy robots and expanding applications in urban low-altitude operations.

When Flying Wasn’t Enough

Skysys’ early products centered on drone docking systems that enabled automated inspection flights in smart-city settings. As AI-based defect detection and alerts were added, the system evolved from a data-collection tool into a more complete inspection platform.

Around 2018 to 2019, the technology began moving into solar farms, where large sites created strong demand for automated inspection. Similar applications later expanded into power distribution, transmission and substations. Rather than simply collecting visual data, the systems could identify defects in solar panels, power-grid equipment and, later, wind turbines without relying on manual review.

From there, the product line increasingly took shape around renewable-energy infrastructure. “Energy is a hard demand regardless of the economic cycle,” co-founder and Chief Scientist Dr. Xiao Suzhi told TechNode. Solar and wind power became key use cases, pushing Skysys’ offerings from general-purpose drone inspection toward specialized solutions for large-scale energy operations.

The Next Step: Action

As drone docking hardware became increasingly commoditized, Skysys saw limited value in competing on hardware alone. More importantly, its deployments revealed another gap: identifying a problem did not necessarily solve it.

Around 2020, the product line began expanding from inspection into maintenance. In solar, for example, drones could locate defects and other issues, but improving power output still required action on the ground. Skysys therefore introduced cleaning and other maintenance robots to extend the workflow from detection to intervention.

“The ultimate goal is still economic value for the customer,” Dr. Xiao said. The products have since evolved around that principle, with maintenance tools designed to improve power generation, reduce safety risks and support long-term asset management.

A Global Market for Solar Maintenance

Skysys is focusing its overseas sales primarily on Europe and the Asia-Pacific region, Wang Xueyan, head of marketing at the company, told TechNode. Its international business has centered on solar inspection and intelligent security, while its newer solar-cleaning robots are being marketed mainly in Europe and Asia-Pacific. On Sept. 17, Skysys was also named to the “2026 AI Going Global Future Unicorn Top 100” list at an event held under the framework of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo.

Wang pointed to several overseas deployments. In Japan, Skysys worked with Huawei on drone-based inspections of mountainous solar farms, using locally deployed computing systems to identify defects such as hot spots, damage, dust and obstructions. In Indonesia, its drones inspect floating solar installations, automatically identifying faults and generating diagnostic reports within about 15 to 20 minutes, replacing labor-intensive inspections previously carried out by boat.

Europe is becoming a key market for Skysys’ solar-cleaning robots, driven by high labor costs and growing demand to improve output from existing rooftop solar assets. Wang said the robots are priced at just over €10,000 for export. In one estimate for an Australian customer, the company calculated that a robot could pay for itself in roughly eight months based on local electricity prices.

The Challenge of Getting Known

As a startup, Skysys has carved out a niche in renewable-energy operations and maintenance through low-altitude intelligence, but limited brand recognition overseas remains a challenge.

“We still need to explore new markets and expand our presence,” Wang said. Skysys’ playbook for overseas expansion is to team up with larger, better-known companies that can help it enter and build new markets.

The data upload controversy surrounding ZCode, an AI coding tool developed by Zhipu AI, is now moving toward a resolution.

On Monday, Zhipu AI announced that ZCode had completed its technical remediation. All cloud data involved in the incident has been deleted, with the deletion verified by two third-party organizations, the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology and NSFOCUS. Zhipu also announced a compensation plan for all users, including free Token credits.

The data security incident, which was first brought to light by the developer community on September 18, has continued for more than 10 days, prompting changes to the product, the release of its source code, and third-party security checks.

The controversy started with a 313MB file

The incident began when developer ferstar was cleaning up files on a local computer. On September 18, the developer discovered an encrypted file of around 313MB in ZCode’s local data directory. Reverse engineering indicated that the file was generated by packaging the user’s entire workspace while logged in.

It contained project source code, Git history, LFS file caches and global development configurations. Developers began questioning how the data was being uploaded. In earlier versions, the feature was enabled by default, while the client did not provide a clear option to disable it.

Some developers reported that even after turning off privacy and indexing-related settings, background processes could continue attempting to upload the data package.

For enterprise developers, the issue went beyond product functionality and raised concerns over code assets and data security. After the incident became public, some companies reportedly stopped using the tool and began checking whether their code had been exposed.

Zhipu responds with a series of changes

Within 72 hours of the incident, Zhipu introduced several changes to ZCode. On September 18, Zhipu issued an apology and acknowledged that the upload mechanism had not been adequately disclosed to users when the feature was initially launched.

On September 19, ZCode released version 3.14.0, removing the Repo Wiki entry as well as the relevant paths for generating and uploading repository snapshots. 

On September 21, Zhipu open-sourced ZCode’s source code and released the results of its first round of third-party security checks. The company said the affected code data had not been retained and had never been used for model training.

In its latest announcement, Zhipu further confirmed that all data objects in the affected Alibaba Cloud OSS bucket, as well as the bucket itself, had been deleted. The deletion was verified by third-party organizations.

Zhipu also said ZCode would adopt a “no upload unless initiated by the user” approach going forward. Unless users actively initiate an upload, code, project files and other development data will remain on local devices and will not be automatically uploaded to the cloud.

The open-source version of ZCode has now been updated to version 3.14.3. Its source code is hosted on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license.

Compensation for all users

Alongside the technical remediation, Zhipu also announced a compensation plan. All paid users will receive four weekly quota reset cards and four five-hour quota reset cards, each valid for one month. From September 28 to October 7, ZCode will also distribute 100,000 free Token packages to all users, with each package containing 100 million Tokens.

The controversy highlights a broader issue facing AI coding tools: as AI becomes increasingly integrated into software development, knowing where users’ code goes can be just as important as the capabilities of the underlying model.

For AI coding tool providers, there needs to be a clear distinction between data uploaded at a user’s request and data transferred automatically in the background. Data collection mechanisms also need to be transparent, with users given clear and verifiable controls over whether their data is uploaded.

The ZCode incident may now be nearing its end, but as AI coding tools become more deeply embedded in enterprise development environments, how to balance AI capabilities, productivity and code security will remain a long-term issue for the industry.

AI-generated video is no longer anything new. But a 100-minute theatrical feature film that uses AI throughout the production process and has secured an official screening license shows how far AI filmmaking has come.

On Sunday, Bona Film Group announced that Sanxingdui: Future Past, China’s first hyper-realistic theatrical film to involve AI throughout the production process, is set to hit cinemas nationwide on October 23, 2026.

The move signals that AI filmmaking is moving beyond lightweight formats such as short videos and online mini-series and into long-form storytelling and the high-production standards of theatrical cinema.

But what makes the film particularly notable is not simply that AI made a movie. The bigger question is whether AI can become part of the production workflow of the film industry.

Making a movie with AI takes more than prompts

Sanxingdui: Future Past runs for 100 minutes and combines the ancient Shu civilization with a futuristic sci-fi setting. All of the film’s characters are original digital creations, with no digital replicas of real actors involved. This approach also avoids issues commonly associated with the use of digital likenesses, such as image-rights authorization.

AI is not acting as an automated director. According to the production team, AI is primarily used for tasks such as image generation and content production, while the creative concept, narrative direction and final artistic decisions remain in the hands of a professional team of more than 100 people at Bona’s AIGMS division, following a conventional film-production workflow.

This highlights one of the biggest challenges facing AI-generated video today: being able to generate a short clip does not mean being able to maintain consistency throughout a feature-length film.

A character may look different from one shot to the next, while facial expressions, movements, costumes and even background details can shift during generation. Such inconsistencies may be manageable in a few-second clip, but they become a much bigger problem in a 100-minute theatrical production.

For this problem, the team did not simply rely on batches of prompts. It manually calibrated details such as characters’ micro-expressions frame by frame to reduce the uncertainty of AI-generated content. The goal was ultimately to meet theatrical production standards, including 4K image quality, high dynamic range color and multi-channel surround sound.

Two years and 1.2 million images: the real challenge is engineering

The production team says the film took two years to make, using more than 1.2 million source images and going through over 100 full-film iterations.

During production, the Infinite Canvas system developed by Boka Film Cloud integrated scripts, storyboards, characters, sets, lighting and other audiovisual assets into a unified creative environment. The approach mirrors a broader trend in AI infrastructure: the challenge is no longer simply generating content, but making the entire production workflow work efficiently.

The same applies to AI filmmaking. Generating an impressive individual shot is becoming increasingly easy. The harder part is maintaining consistency in characters, environments, lighting and visual language across a 100-minute film.

That means the future of AI filmmaking may depend not only on model capabilities, but also on an entire workflow covering asset management, content collaboration, version control and human supervision.

Sanxingdui meets super AI — and AI becomes part of the story

The film’s plot revolves around mysteries left behind by the Sanxingdui civilization. According to the story, mysterious symbols found on Sanxingdui bronzeware conceal a binary code that could not have originated 3,000 years ago.

In the future, super AI spreads across the world, and humans increasingly hand over their decisions and judgment to algorithms, eventually triggering a systemic crisis.

Iconic Sanxingdui artifacts, including the Bronze Sacred Tree, Bronze Standing Figure and Bronze Masks with protruding eyes, will be brought to life in a futuristic sci-fi setting. 

Interestingly, AI is not only a production tool in the film. It is also one of the central themes of the story itself. As humans become increasingly dependent on algorithms to make decisions, how can we preserve our own ability to judge and choose?

The film previously made appearances at the Cannes Film Festival and the Hong Kong International Film & TV Market, where it also released an international concept trailer.

AI filmmaking is going through a clear evolution — from several-second visual demos to short videos, advertising and online series, and now to theatrical feature films.

Being able to generate is only the first step. Being able to generate long-form content consistently and eventually integrate AI into an industrial-scale production workflow is the bigger challenge for AI filmmaking.

Whether Sanxingdui: Future Past can make that model work will only become clear after its theatrical release on October 23. But at the very least, the film is pushing AI filmmaking beyond the question of whether it can be done, toward a more fundamental one: can AI become part of the film industry itself?

DragonLab is TechNode’s effort to close that gap, looking past the noise to discover China’s next wave of innovation—emerging companies, ambitious founders, and breakthrough technologies that have yet to receive global attention.

Making a video game has traditionally been a complex process involving multiple specialized roles. Designers create concepts and gameplay systems, programmers build mechanics, artists develop characters and environments, and producers coordinate development and iteration.

Over the past two decades, several companies have tried to make game creation more accessible. Professional engines such as Unity and Unreal Engine have given smaller teams access to powerful development tools, while no-code platforms have helped people without programming backgrounds experiment with making games.

Now, a new generation of startups is exploring a more ambitious idea: what if creating a game could begin with an idea described in words, rather than years of learning development tools?

That is the vision behind JIYI’s SOON, an AI-powered game creation platform designed to help users turn creative ideas into playable game experiences.

The company is exploring whether AI can take on more of the work traditionally handled by game designers, artists, and programmers. It hopes to help creators move from an idea to a playable prototype much faster.

The ambition behind SOON can be summed up in a simple phrase: a game studio in minutes.

From No-Code Engines to Ai-Powered Creation

To understand what SOON is trying to change, it helps to look at an earlier effort to make game development easier: GDevelop.

GDevelop began as an open-source project in 2008. The company behind it, GDevelop France, was incorporated in 2021 and is based in Paris. It has since grown into a no-code game engine aimed at people who want to make games without first learning a traditional programming language. Instead of requiring users to write most game logic in code, it provides a visual, event-based system for building interactions and gameplay. The platform lets creators publish games across web, desktop and mobile platforms.

That makes GDevelop a useful reference point for SOON. Long before generative AI became part of game development, GDevelop was already tackling the same broad problem: how to let more people make games.

Its answer was to simplify the development environment. Users still build scenes, define events, set behaviors and make design decisions themselves, but they can do so without mastering conventional programming. GDevelop has since added AI features as another layer of assistance, while remaining fundamentally a game engine that creators operate.

SOON starts from the same desire to lower the barrier, but pushes the idea further. Rather than simply making an engine easier to use, it aims to reduce the amount of manual work a creator performs inside that engine-like workflow. The platform presents natural-language interaction as a way to move from an initial idea toward a playable game, with AI taking on more of the execution.

For now, SOON is focused largely on 2D and mini-game projects, a deliberate trade-off that lets it use a more constrained framework to automate more of the production process while keeping output relatively stable. That makes it narrower than GDevelop, which supports both 2D and 3D development, but also reflects SOON’s strategy of going deeper on AI-driven game generation rather than trying to match the breadth of a general-purpose engine.

GDevelop already lowers the technical barrier to game development by removing much of the need for traditional coding. But creators still need to learn how its engine works, structure game logic, manage assets, and assemble the game themselves. SOON is trying to lower that barrier further, allowing users to describe what they want while AI takes on more of the production work.

Large commercial games still depend on experienced teams, precise control, and sophisticated development environments. But for prototypes, small projects, and creator-driven games, SOON is already showing what its approach can do. During its second round of testing, users created more than 3,000 game projects in 45 days, with the platform helping generate code, game logic, characters, scenes, and UI.

A Startup Emerging From the Gaming Ecosystem

Many AI gaming startups in the U.S. have emerged from software or AI research backgrounds, focusing on areas such as AI characters, interactive agents, and generative content. Inworld AI, for example, provides tools for adding intelligent characters, voice, and real-time interactions to games built with engines such as Unreal and Unity.

JIYI’s background is different. The company operates within China’s gaming and technology ecosystem, where developers and investors are exploring AI as a way to reduce the cost and complexity of game production.

In this context, JIYI has positioned SOON as an AI game-creation platform. Its approach reflects a question increasingly facing the gaming industry: Will AI remain another tool in the developer’s toolkit, or will it reshape the way games are produced? SOON is placing its bet on the latter.

JIYI was incubated by Chinese gaming company Kingnet Network and has since attracted investment from Bingo Group, Zhongxu Future and Hengdian Capital. In 2026, the company had raised nearly RMB 100 million ($14 million) across two funding rounds.

China is one of the world’s largest video-game markets, with a substantial domestic development and publishing industry. That gives startups like JIYI a large pool of developers, publishers, investors, and production experience to draw from as they experiment with new ways of making games.

SOON has also begun to attract industry recognition. At the 2025 China International Artificial Intelligence Conference, it was named one of the year’s 10 most innovative AI products, alongside products from companies including Huawei, JD Logistics, and Inspur Cloud. In July 2026, SOON was named Best AI Game Creation Platform at the seventh Feifan Awards, which focuses on the commercial application of AI.

JIYI’s pitch is ultimately about production efficiency. SOON aims to compress more of the game-making process into a single platform, helping smaller teams and individual creators move from an idea to a playable project with fewer steps.

Beyond game creation, in a strategic partnership with CMGE, the company launched GamePartner.AI, an AI-powered agent designed to help developers publish games to platforms including Apple’s App Store and Google Play, while connecting them with advertising monetization services such as AppLovin.

The Rise of the One-Person Game Studio

One of the most interesting ideas behind AI game creation is the possibility of smaller teams and individual creators producing more ambitious projects.

Traditional game development is often limited by resources. A creator may have a strong idea but lack the programming, art, or design skills needed to turn that idea into a finished product.

AI tools could change that balance. A creator who previously needed several specialists may be able to use AI to generate early versions, test concepts quickly, and refine ideas at a lower cost.

The trend resembles changes seen in other creative industries. Digital cameras, editing software and online publishing platforms lowered barriers to creating and distributing photography and video, giving independent creators direct access to tools and audiences that were once harder to reach.

Game development may be heading in a similar direction. If tools like SOON can take over more of the technical work, people with ideas but little development experience could have a much easier path to making something playable.

The Challenge: Creating Games People Want to Play

Generating a game is much harder than generating an individual asset. A successful game depends on how its mechanics, pacing, challenge and feedback come together to keep players engaged.

Some platforms like Meshy in the U.S. and Hyper3D’s Rodin in China, largely focus on helping developers create characters, props, environments, textures, and other production-ready assets. These tools can save artists and studios significant time while fitting into existing game-development workflows.

SOON, on the other side, takes a broader approach, bringing code, game logic, characters, scenes, and UI into the same creation process with the goal of producing a playable project.

Some companies are also expanding beyond asset generation into interactive environments and world-building. Tripo AI, for example, is developing persistent multiplayer worlds through Project Eden, while Runway has been exploring real-time, AI-generated game worlds that respond to player input.

a successful game requires much more than characters, environments, or code. It needs compelling gameplay, balance, progression, storytelling, and a reason for players to return. Research on game design and player experience has repeatedly emphasized the importance of factors such as challenge, feedback, immersion, and engagement.

For tools like SOON, one of the current questions is how to turn those generated pieces into an experience that feels coherent and keeps players interested.

A New Chapter for Game Creation

For years, platforms such as GDevelop have widened access to game development by making the tools easier to use. SOON is pushing that idea further, giving AI a larger role in the work that happens between an initial concept and a playable game.

The platform is still being developed, and large commercial titles will continue to rely on experienced teams and sophisticated production tools. But SOON points to a different kind of creator workflow, one where people can describe what they want, see a playable result quickly, and then shape it through further instructions.

That could make game creation accessible to people who have ideas but little experience with coding, engines, or production pipelines. For them, making a game may start less with learning a tool and more with simply trying an idea.

If the keyword for AI infrastructure over the past few years was simply more compute, the large-scale deployment of Agentic AI is forcing the industry to confront a more practical question: How efficiently can all that compute actually be used?

At the 2026 Apsara Conference, H3C put the question in terms of Tokens. As AI agents continuously call on foundation models, trillion-Token-scale services are emerging as a new infrastructure requirement.

Simply adding more GPUs does not necessarily deliver proportional performance gains. Idle compute, network congestion, insufficient data supply, and the operational and failure challenges of large-scale clusters can all erode the value of additional compute.

That is why H3C’s product lineup at the event, while spanning a wide range of technologies, follows a relatively clear logic: from compute to networking and storage, and from software to operations, AI infrastructure is moving beyond hardware stacking toward system-level optimization.

More GPUs do not necessarily mean more performance

Zhu Shiyin, general manager of H3C’s Advanced Technology Research Department, described AI clusters as highly integrated systems that require close hardware-software coordination.

As cluster sizes grow from hundreds of GPUs to thousands or even tens of thousands, GPUs themselves become just one part of the equation. Chip-to-chip communication, data transfer, task scheduling, power supply, and cooling can all directly affect overall compute utilization.

H3C’s UniPoD S80000 Series SuperPod, showcased at the event, reflects this approach. It supports configurations ranging from 32 to 1,024 GPUs and can scale further to 16,384 GPUs, while supporting heterogeneous computing resources including CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, and DPUs and mainstream frameworks.

The focus is not simply on putting more chips into a single system, but on coordinating compute, networking, storage, cloud, security, and operations so that different types of computing resources can be managed as a unified system.

In other words, the competition in AI clusters is shifting from how many GPUs a system has to how many useful Tokens each GPU can actually produce.

As GPUs get faster, the network can become the bottleneck

Zhu also highlighted high-speed interconnects, an increasingly important part of AI infrastructure. The reason is straightforward: as GPU performance improves, the amount of data exchanged between GPUs also grows. If the network cannot keep up, GPUs are forced to wait.

This is why H3C showcased three interconnect scenarios at the event: Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across.

Within a node, H3C introduced the S9828-128EO, a 102.4T NPO silicon-photonics intelligent computing switch that uses co-packaged optics to reduce end-to-end latency by 15%. Between nodes, the company’s 1.6T intelligent computing switch S9828-64FP, adopts 224G SerDes technologies, it cuts power consumption by more than 20% in high-density environments to support large-scale cluster expansion.

Across data centers, the 800G intelligent computing DCI switch S12500R-64EP is designed to support intra-city cross-data-center compute scheduling and gradient synchronization.

The logic behind these three layers comes down to a core question: As AI clusters grow, how can interconnects avoid becoming the brakes on compute performance?

Interconnects are also no longer simply a matter of bandwidth. As clusters expand, protocols, congestion control, link reliability, and fault diagnosis become equally important. If vendors develop closed technical ecosystems independently, they could create new technology silos. Open protocols and industry standards will therefore become increasingly important.

Beyond compute, there is another frequently underestimated challenge: data

GPUs cannot run without data. In large-model training, data preparation, model training, and parameter exchange all involve massive amounts of data movement. During inference, KV Cache adds further pressure on storage and caching resources.

H3C therefore also positioned high-performance storage as part of the broader Token production pipeline. Its UniStor X20000 series X20836 can deliver up to 200GB/s of bandwidth and 3 million IOPS per node, while supporting interoperability across block, file, object, and HDFS protocols.

According to H3C, its full-speed engine can reduce GPU waiting time by 30%, while XCache inference acceleration can cut time-to-first-token latency by up to 90% in inference scenarios.

The takeaway is fairly practical: AI infrastructure is evolving from a compute center into a comprehensive data processing system. From data preparation and training to inference and Token generation, every period of waiting ultimately translates into cost.

Software may be the next battleground

Once hardware reaches a certain scale, software optimization becomes increasingly important. Zhu noted that everything from the operating system and communication libraries to resource management and scheduling platforms needs to work closely with the underlying hardware.

Communication optimization, overlapping computation with communication, task scheduling, dynamic load balancing, and unified resource management can all help reduce GPU idle time and communication conflicts.

This is also why modern AI infrastructure increasingly resembles a super-system. Chips provide compute, networks connect resources, storage supplies data, and power and cooling keep the system running. Software, meanwhile, is responsible for orchestrating these resources into a functioning whole.

If any one of these components becomes a bottleneck, the impact is no longer limited to a single hardware metric. It ultimately affects how many useful Tokens the system can generate per second and how much each Token costs to produce.

The next phase of AI infrastructure is a competition over compute utilization

From H3C’s exhibition booth to its forum sessions at the Apsara Conference, the company was essentially making the same point from different angles.

Supernodes address how compute resources can be organized at scale. High-speed networking addresses how those resources can communicate efficiently. High-performance storage ensures that data can be delivered in time. Software, scheduling, operations, and unified management then turn these resources into AI capabilities that can be used continuously and efficiently.

The next phase of competition in AI infrastructure, therefore, may not be determined simply by who has more GPUs. As model sizes reach the trillion-parameter scale and AI agents increasingly call foundation models, metrics such as compute utilization, Token throughput, latency, energy consumption, and cost per Token are becoming increasingly important.

That is the deeper meaning behind the pursuit of extreme Token cost efficiency: it is not about putting more GPUs together, but about making every GPU, every network link, and every unit of storage in the system spend less time waiting and more time working.

As AI enters the stage of large-scale production, compute is no longer just a chip problem. It is becoming a competition over the efficiency of the entire infrastructure system.
