]]> 198739 Apple iPhone Duo joins the foldable phone market: do Chinese brands still have the edge? https://technode.com/2026/09/11/apple-joins-the-foldable-phone-market-do-chinese-brands-still-have-the-edge/ Fri, 11 Sep 2026 09:02:31 +0000 https://technode.com/?p=198725 Apple has finally entered the foldable smartphone market. This week, Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, with a starting price of $1,999. The device features a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded and a 5.4-inch outer display when folded. It is powered by the A20 Pro chip, supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, […]]]>

Apple has finally entered the foldable smartphone market. This week, Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, with a starting price of $1,999. The device features a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded and a 5.4-inch outer display when folded.

It is powered by the A20 Pro chip, supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, and offers up to 2TB of storage. Apple also highlighted a new precision hinge, a reduced-crease design, and an iOS experience optimized specifically for the foldable form factor.

Apple’s promotional video also reveals how the company wants consumers to think about the foldable form factor. Through a series of fast and highly stylized scene transitions, the iPhone Duo moves between different scenarios as it folds and unfolds, making the change in form feel almost seamless.

The focus is not simply on the mechanical act of folding the phone, but on how that change can alter the user’s interaction with the device. In that sense, Apple is presenting the foldable iPhone less as a new type of hardware and more as a phone that can adapt its form to different situations.

For Apple, the launch represents one of the biggest changes to the iPhone’s form factor in more than a decade. But in China, Apple is not entering an empty market.

Chinese smartphone makers including Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo have been competing in the foldable segment for years. They have released multiple generations of foldable phones while continuously working to reduce weight and thickness and improve hinges, display creases, battery life, and software optimization for larger screens.

As Apple begins to explore what a foldable iPhone should look like, Chinese manufacturers are already asking what the next generation of foldable phones should look like.

Apple takes a relatively mature approach

The iPhone Duo does not take the most aggressive approach. It adopts the book-style horizontal fold that has become one of the more established designs in the market. Its 7.6-inch inner display offers a screen size close to that of a small tablet when unfolded, while the 5.4-inch outer display is designed for everyday smartphone use. Apple says the two displays use consistent proportions to ensure that content can transition smoothly between the folded and unfolded states.

This design has already gone through several generations of development in China. For example, Huawei’s Mate X7 features an 8-inch inner display and a 6.49-inch outer display. It is about 9.5mm thick when folded and weighs around 235 grams.

Oppo’s Find N6 features an 8.12-inch inner display and a 6.62-inch outer display, measuring about 8.93mm thick when folded and weighing around 225 grams. The Vivo X Fold6 features an 8.02-inch inner display and a 6.51-inch outer display, with a weight starting at around 228 grams.

By comparison, the iPhone Duo weighs around 254 grams and measures 11.3mm thick when folded, making it heavier and thicker than the three Chinese foldable phones mentioned above.

This points to an interesting reality: when Apple is making its first foldable phone, Chinese manufacturers have moved the competition beyond whether a phone can fold to whether a foldable can be as thin and light as a conventional smartphone.

Still, weight alone does not determine the overall user experience. Apple has its own advantages in structural design, hinges, and display technology. The company also says the Duo is the thinnest iPhone ever when unfolded (5.2mm thick) and uses a new hinge and display design to reduce the visibility of the crease.

But in terms of hardware iteration, Chinese smartphone makers clearly have more experience with foldable devices.

The real competition may be software

However, looking only at hardware specifications could underestimate the significance of Apple’s entry. The biggest challenge for foldable phones has never been just the hinge or the display. It is how to make the larger screen genuinely useful.

The iPhone Duo introduces split-screen multitasking for its larger display and supports Apple Pencil. Apple is hoping that users will be able to handle multiple tasks when the phone is unfolded, rather than simply seeing an enlarged version of the standard iPhone interface.

Chinese manufacturers are exploring the same direction. The Vivo X Fold6 features an 8.02-inch inner display and supports multitasking on the larger screen. Oppo’s Find N6 goes further by positioning itself as a Pocket AI Workstation, supporting multiple apps running simultaneously, adjustable windows, and desktop-style multitasking features such as Split View.

Huawei has also added features such as split-screen translation, split-screen navigation, AI call summaries, AI call translation, and multi-device collaboration to the Mate XT 2, turning its tri-fold design into more than just a larger display and positioning it as an AI and productivity tool.

Therefore, the real competition Apple faces is not simply who has the larger screen, but who can actually change the way consumers use their phones.

Apple has an ecosystem advantage Chinese brands cannot easily replicate

Apple also has an advantage that Chinese smartphone makers will find difficult to replicate: a tightly integrated hardware and software ecosystem. The A20 Pro chip, iOS, Apple Pencil, and integration across the iPhone, iPad, and Mac could all become important selling points for the foldable iPhone.

For users who already own an iPhone, Mac, or iPad, buying a foldable iPhone is not simply about purchasing another smartphone. It could introduce a new way of interacting with their existing devices. This also helps explain why Apple can afford to enter the foldable market years after other manufacturers.

It does not need to prove that there is demand for foldable phones. Chinese manufacturers, along with Samsung and others, have already helped establish the category. What Apple needs to prove is whether a foldable can become the next iPhone, rather than simply a more expensive iPhone.

Apple is the newcomer, but Chinese brands face new challenges

Apple’s entry into the foldable market cuts both ways. For Chinese manufacturers, Apple represents a new competitor. With its strong brand, massive user base, and mature developer ecosystem, Apple could help push foldable phones further into the mainstream if the foldable iPhone gains traction.

At the same time, Apple’s entry could also validate years of experimentation by Chinese manufacturers. By the time Apple entered the foldable market, Huawei was already exploring tri-fold designs, Oppo was continuing to reduce the weight and visibility of creases on its foldables, and Vivo was exploring AI and productivity features for large screens.

So this is not simply a competition between Apple and Chinese smartphone brands. More accurately, it is a collision between two different product approaches: Apple is looking to redefine the foldable experience through its mature ecosystem and software, while Chinese manufacturers are drawing on years of hardware iteration to explore how much further foldable phones can go.

Apple may have entered the foldable race late, but it has changed the question for everyone else. For Chinese smartphone makers, the challenge is no longer simply to make foldables thinner, lighter, or more advanced. It is to keep finding new ways to make the form factor useful — and convince consumers that a foldable phone can be more than just a phone that folds.

Zhanbolat Kakishev, Chief Product Officer of the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), believes that perception is beginning to change. “Traditionally, China always looked into the advanced economies—Europe, America, Australia, Canada—and tried to do business and build […]]]>

For many Chinese investors, Kazakhstan and Central Asia have long been associated with natural resources—oil, gas, mining and commodities.

Zhanbolat Kakishev, Chief Product Officer of the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), believes that perception is beginning to change.

“Traditionally, China always looked into the advanced economies—Europe, America, Australia, Canada—and tried to do business and build production there because they would like to be closer to the international customer,” Kakishev told TechNode in Astana.

“But I think Central Asia was always skipped and overlooked,” he said. “We were only considered to be a natural-resources type play.”

Kakishev argues that Kazakhstan today offers more than resources. With access to Eurasian markets, investment incentives and special economic zones, he believes AIFC can serve as a platform for Chinese companies seeking international expansion.

Building a common-law financial center in Astana

AIFC was established as a financial center with its own legal and regulatory framework.

“We are set up as a common law jurisdiction,” Kakishev said.

The center has its own regulator, the Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA), as well as its own court and arbitration system. Its court includes English judges, with a former Chief Justice of England and Wales serving as chairman.

AIFC also operates the Astana International Exchange (AIX), which focuses on international currencies within the common-law framework, while Kazakhstan’s stock exchange in Almaty mainly handles tenge-denominated securities.

According to Kakishev, AIFC offers corporate structures including partnerships, private and public companies, foundations and trusts.

“We are quite business oriented,” he said, noting that AIFC can adjust regulations faster than national legislative processes.

AIFC had surpassed 6,200 registered companies at the time of the interview and provides an Expat Centre that Kakishev described as a “one-stop shop,” offering around 120 services including visa support.

From finance to AI infrastructure

As Chief Product Officer, Kakishev oversees new financial products and investment initiatives within AIFC.

One focus is aviation finance. Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan are expected to lease around 300 new aircraft over the next four years, and AIFC is developing a framework to attract aviation leasing companies while exploring sustainable aviation fuel.

The center is also expanding into green finance, renewable energy certificates and carbon markets. Kakishev said Kazakhstan’s large land area creates opportunities for nature-based projects.

Islamic finance is another area of development. “We have both Malaysian and Arabic scholars within our organization,” he said. “We came up with a framework which we believe actually reconciles both.”

AIFC is also examining Kazakhstan’s role in artificial intelligence. Kakishev said the country may not compete directly in large language models.

“We realized that Kazakhstan probably is too late on the large language models application,” he said.

Instead, he believes Kazakhstan could find opportunities in AI infrastructure. “We see a lot of potential for Kazakhstan to play in the infrastructure space, building data centers.”

Turning resources and ideas into investable opportunities

While mining remains central to Kazakhstan’s economy, AIFC is working to address financing gaps in the sector.

Kakishev pointed to a dual IPO with Hong Kong involving Jiaxin International Resources Investment Limited as an example. “We would like to have more Jiaxins,” he said.

AIFC is developing a junior mining platform where exploration companies can present projects to investors after preliminary assessments. “We are acting as a centralized depository for all junior mining opportunities,” Kakishev said.

The center is applying similar financial structures to creative industries, allowing filmmakers and musicians to establish investment vehicles through AIFC.

“For international players, it’s also easier to invest when there is a proper common-law GP-LP kind of structure,” he said.

China, Hong Kong and Kazakhstan’s next phase

For Kakishev, China and Hong Kong are natural partners in Kazakhstan’s development. “I think China, including Hong Kong, is a natural fit with the opportunities which exist in Kazakhstan,” he said.

He sees Hong Kong as a source of capital and financial expertise, while China can contribute manufacturing and technology capabilities. “The third dimension I would mention is the technology transfer,” Kakishev said. “We don’t want only investments; we want capabilities.”

He highlighted areas including automobile manufacturing, advanced manufacturing, composites and critical minerals. “We would like to use that capability and create a win-win situation for both of the countries,” he said.

Kazakhstan as a testing ground for startups

Kakishev also believes Kazakhstan could become a launchpad for Chinese technology companies expanding overseas. “Technology companies usually want to scale,” he said.

Rather than immediately entering highly competitive markets, startups could use Kazakhstan and Eurasia as a testing environment. “We think that Kazakhstan market, Eurasian market, in its own right, can be a good piloting stage,” Kakishev said.

“Kazakhstan was always at the crossroads, uniting Europe, China, north Russia, and some of the Arabic culture as well, because of the historical heritage,” he said.

“People here understand different cultures, and it’s a good place to test your hypotheses and pivot your startup into a new geographic location,” he said.

For Kakishev, China-Kazakhstan cooperation has two major tracks: government digitalization and startup ecosystem development. “I definitely believe there is both big partnerships, win-win, both in the government sector as well as the private sector,” he said.

For Chinese companies looking beyond traditional markets, Kazakhstan wants to be seen not only as a source of resources, but as a financial hub, technology partner and testing ground for global expansion.

Kazakhstan’s venture capital ecosystem is still young, but Askar Bilisbekov, CEO and board member of Alem Capital Management, sees room for growth through more institutional capital, stronger international links and deeper ties with China.

“We’re still building our ecosystem,” Bilisbekov told TechNode in Astana. “Lots of missing parts in our ecosystem.”

Those gaps include M&A and capital markets, while venture capital itself remains unfamiliar to many local investors. Still, Bilisbekov sees growing interest beyond Kazakhstan’s traditional oil and gas industries, including private equity, critical minerals and technology.

BUILDING CAPITAL — AND HELPING STARTUPS SCALE

Bilisbekov describes Alem Capital not simply as a fund, but as an “investment platform.” The government-backed initiative received its license in July 2025 and completed its first closing that October, raising $115 million across two funds: $95 million for venture capital and $20 million for crypto. Roughly two-thirds of its capital comes from the private sector.

“We started our deployment process officially” this year, Bilisbekov said.

Alem Capital has selected six funds across its first two cohorts and plans additional funds focused on energy alternatives and AI data centers, with a target size of $1 billion. Its mandate covers Kazakhstan, Central Asia, the Caucasus and global investments, although Kazakhstan remains the primary focus.

For Bilisbekov, the challenge is not simply a lack of money. “It’s not because we’re lacking in capital here; it’s more on the awareness of the asset class itself,” he said. “If you don’t know the asset class, you don’t invest there.”

But startups face another obstacle: scale. Kazakhstan and other former Soviet markets remain fragmented, Bilisbekov said. Local founders are expanding into the United States, Europe and Africa, but China remains less explored.

“Nobody is thinking that we can do an expanded opportunity in China,” he said.

“If we do cross-border development, founders coming from China here, and our founders going to China, I think that’s another opportunity to look into bigger opportunities to scale,” he said.

BUILDING A VC BRIDGE WITH CHINA

Alem Capital has organized an LP-GP Summit for two consecutive years, bringing international investors into Kazakhstan’s technology ecosystem, including Chinese VCs.

“I want to see them more,” Bilisbekov said. “Sharing the same borders and being close neighbors and allies, we have to expand our economic development in the space where I’m currently working: VC and private equity.”

He also sees opportunities for Chinese deep-tech companies because of Kazakhstan’s STEM talent, scientific institutions and laboratories.

“Of course, hundred percent,” Bilisbekov said when asked whether Chinese companies in robotics, AI hardware, batteries and energy could find opportunities in the country.

“I think that’s also a good foundation for any deep-tech startups or deep-tech projects to roll out their operations here in Kazakhstan.”

Why Kazakhstan could appeal to global investors

Bilisbekov puts political stability and neutrality at the top of Kazakhstan’s investment pitch.

“Kazakhstan’s number one thing is our political stability and our neutrality.”

He described the country as being “like a Switzerland in Asian markets,” citing its relationships with China, Russia, the United States, Europe and the United Kingdom. He also highlighted the Astana International Financial Centre and its independent court and common-law framework.

“Any investor wants to come to a country where his or her rights are protected,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s digitalization is another advantage. Bilisbekov said government services and financial transactions can increasingly be handled by phone, while internet coverage is close to 90%.

“I don’t bring any ID. I have everything on my phone,” he said. “You see, that’s the level of digitalization of our country.”

He also pointed to more than 5,000 startups, Astana Hub’s growing role, and sectors including fintech, agritech and spacetech. Robotics could also become important, with Bilisbekov expecting a “super cycle” driven by AI and robotics.

For Bilisbekov, however, the strongest case for Kazakhstan is made in person.

“Come to our country to see with your own eyes what kind of opportunities we have,” he said. “My opinion is the opinion of one person. You’re gonna find opinions of different people.”

Kazakhstan’s venture ecosystem is still developing, but Bilisbekov believes more capital, more founders and stronger international links — particularly with China — could help shape its next phase of growth.

Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

The first time many people saw a humanoid robot, it was probably doing something impressive: dancing, flipping, or performing a carefully rehearsed routine. The industry’s biggest challenge now lies in turning those impressive demonstrations into robots that can perform useful tasks in everyday environments.

That is the challenge facing China’s rapidly growing humanoid robot industry. As companies move from demonstrations toward commercial deployment, they are exploring how these machines can take on practical roles in workplaces, services and other real-world settings.

Chinese companies are moving faster and at greater scale than U.S. rivals at this stage, Selina Xu, China and AI policy lead in Eric Schmidt’s office, told TechCrunch. But when does the sector get its “ChatGPT moment” — the breakthrough Sam Altman says could be just a few years away?

The Story Behind China’s Dominance

Three forces are giving China an early edge: cost, capital and a large testing ground for commercialization. Its manufacturing base, reinforced by the EV supply chain for batteries, sensors and other components, lets robot makers source hardware locally, iterate faster and lower prices. In the first half of 2026, five Chinese companies accounted for 86% of global humanoid shipments, according to Counterpoint Research.

Funding is another factor. XPeng’s robotics unit raised more than $900 million in August, valuing it at more than $6.3 billion. Galbot raised RMB 2.5 billion ($362 million) in March after a $300 million-plus round in late 2025 valued it at about $3 billion.

China also offers a broad range of potential markets. Humanoids are being deployed or tested in automotive manufacturing, electronics, logistics, aerospace and energy. But commercialization remains early, with deployments ranging from purchases to preorders and pilots, while large-scale repeat orders remain limited.

The Hard Part of the Robot Boom

China’s humanoid makers still face questions over AI systems and integrated software. Vision-language-action models and world models remain early, while Nvidia leads with an end-to-end robotics software stack, leaving many Chinese startups reliant on its Orin chips even as domestic chipmakers develop alternatives.

The harder test is turning physical capability into sustainable commercial demand. Jiang Han, a senior researcher at the Pangoal Institution, told TechNode that repeat orders and customer payback periods are key signs that robots are solving real problems rather than simply attracting trial use. He said China’s longer-term advantage lies not in low manufacturing costs alone, but in combining supply-chain cost advantages with rapid hardware and algorithm iteration.

Data remains another bottleneck. Unlike large language models, robot developers cannot simply scrape the internet for examples of physical interaction. They are turning to synthetic data, simulation, reinforcement learning and real-world deployments. Harry Mellsop, co-founder of Antioch, a startup building simulation tools for physical AI, has described physical AI as being in its “GPT-2 era,” referring to the OpenAI model that predated ChatGPT, with more data and computing power still needed.

Reliability can break an otherwise impressive demo. Speaking at BEYOND Expo, Fu Sheng, chairman and CEO of Cheetah Mobile and chairman of service robotics company OrionStar, said robotics’ hardest challenge is “the last 1%”: a 99% success rate still means one failure in every 100 attempts. He argued that commercial robots must prove they can operate reliably and efficiently over long periods before they become useful workers.

Safety and security add another hurdle. A high-profile accident could trigger public backlash as deployment accelerates. Jiang also pointed to supply-chain vulnerabilities and data-security compliance as gaps Chinese robot makers still need to address, particularly in European and U.S. markets.

Useful First, General Later

Yuli Zhao, chief strategy officer at Galbot, a Chinese humanoid robotics startup that focuses on embodied intelligence and commercial deployment, expects demand to emerge first in manufacturing, warehouse logistics and retail, where tasks are repetitive and workflows are clear — conditions he said create real demand and give humanoid robots a better chance to deliver value at scale.

Fu makes a similar case for specialization. Rather than chasing a general-purpose robot, he argued that companies may find more commercial value in well-defined jobs such as agriculture, transport and sorting, then improve reliability, efficiency and deployment around those tasks.

But the longer-term goal remains general intelligence. Jiang said a true “ChatGPT moment” would require a general embodied-intelligence model that can understand natural-language instructions and break complex tasks into steps rather than rely on preprogrammed actions. The key bottleneck, he said, is handling long-tail situations in unstructured environments, where robots can still fail when something unfamiliar happens.

China may be well positioned to run that cycle quickly. Zhao described its advantage as “speed-to-scale,” with R&D, supply chains, manufacturing, integration and deployment operating in a tight loop — moving robots from prototypes into real-world use faster and feeding operational data into the next round of development.

On Tuesday, XPeng announced that its automated production line for humanoid robots had begun operations. The first IRON humanoid robot completed the automated final assembly process and autonomously walked off the production line, marking the company’s move from the R&D stage toward mass production.

XPeng said IRON is the world’s first high-level general-purpose humanoid robot to be produced on an automated production line.

The production line was designed and built by XPeng’s own team. According to the company, it incorporates manufacturing and quality-control systems developed for the automotive industry, while adapting them to the precision and flexibility required for humanoid robot assembly. More than 80% of the line’s core processes are automated, XPeng said.

Humanoid robots are still in the early stages of commercialization, with most products yet to reach large-scale production and manufacturing processes still involving significant amounts of manual assembly.

Automated production lines could improve manufacturing efficiency and product consistency while providing a foundation for scaling output. However, humanoid robots involve a large number of precision components and complex mechanical systems, meaning automotive manufacturing practices cannot be directly applied in every aspect. The actual efficiency and cost of mass production remain to be tested.

IRON is part of XPeng’s physical AI strategy and is positioned as a general-purpose humanoid robot. The company aims to develop a unified hardware and software platform that will allow the robot to operate across different real-world environments and perform a range of tasks.

IRON features a fully enclosed flexible lattice structure and has 76 degrees of freedom across its body, including 21 in its hands. The robot is equipped with three Turing AI chips, providing up to 2,250 TOPS of effective computing power, according to XPeng. The company said its physical AI model can run locally on the robot, allowing it to perceive its surroundings and perform tasks without relying on remote human control.

Under XPeng’s current product roadmap, IRON is expected to enter scaled production by the end of 2026 and begin commercial deliveries in 2027. The company expects the robot to initially take on dangerous and highly repetitive tasks before expanding into a wider range of real-world applications.

XPeng has also been stepping up efforts to commercialize its robotics business. The company recently completed its first funding round for the robotics business, raising more than $900 million at a post-money valuation of over $6.3 billion.

According to the company, the latest funding round was led by IDG Capital, with Gaorong Capital participating. It also received strategic investment from Tencent and Alibaba. XPeng Group will continue to retain control of its robotics business.

He Xiaopeng, CEO of XPeng, said the company aims to bring its humanoid robots into the real world in the not-too-distant future.

He said XPeng’s robots would be “more human-like and safer,” require no remote control, support natural interaction and have their own memory. More importantly, he said the goal is not to build robots for demonstrations, but to create products that can deliver real value and achieve mass production.

At an SCMP Live panel in Astana, representatives of AIX, HKEX, Alem Capital Management and Gobi Partners discussed how Central Asian companies could connect with international capital, and what a more diversified route beyond traditional resource and trade links might require.

Central Asia sits between China, Russia, Europe and the Middle East and has long been viewed through the Silk Road, natural resources and trade routes.

For Kazakhstan today, another question is emerging: how can companies in the region connect more directly with international capital?

That question framed “Capital Pathways for Central Asia – Dual Listings, RMB Funding, Private Capital and the Astana-Hong Kong Route.” Speakers included Assel Mukazhanova of AIX, Johnson Chui of HKEX, Askar Bilisbekov of Alem Capital Management and Thomas G. Tsao of Gobi Partners, with SCMP’s Eugene Tang moderating.

Why Kazakhstan Is Looking Outward

For Assel Mukazhanova, the starting point is companies’ financing needs.

“I think the most important thing is that we look at the needs of our clients,” the AIX chief executive said, referring to companies seeking to raise capital internationally.

Investment banks are central to that process, Mukazhanova said, because they know investors’ appetite and can help companies choose which market to approach.

Kazakhstan’s natural-resource base creates financing demand that the domestic market cannot necessarily meet, pushing AIX to seek links with other financial centres.

“We would like to connect with as many financial centers as possible,” Mukazhanova said.

Interest in Hong Kong was visible at the event, where companies were exploring its stock market as one possible route to international capital.

Regulatory Familiarity and Private Capital

Thomas G. Tsao argued that Hong Kong could give frontier-market companies greater investor confidence.

Comparing the situation with an earlier generation of Chinese startups, Tsao said, “It was like why in the old days a lot of Chinese startups wanted to list on Nasdaq. It was because of the perceived and actual regulatory standards.”

He sees a similar effect potentially emerging around Hong Kong: “I think right now Hong Kong Stock Exchange… they raise the bar. And so I think for Kazakhstan startups, going to Hong Kong, there is that halo.”

For investors unfamiliar with a startup’s jurisdiction, that familiarity can matter. Tsao said Hong Kong can make companies easier to approach because “people are more familiar” with its regulatory regime.

Askar Bilisbekov brought the private-market perspective. Alem Capital Management is running two funds, including a venture capital fund investing in funds regionally and globally, and plans an infrastructure fund.

“My space is venture capital, private,” Bilisbekov said, noting that he was not yet focused on the IPO space.

Together, the comments pointed to a financing landscape in which private funds, investment banks and public markets can serve different stages of a company’s growth.

People and Cross-Border Networks

For Kazakhstan, however, those connections still depend on whether companies can meet the requirements of each market and find investors for a specific stage of growth.

What a Capital Bridge Still Requires

A panelist responded that access through Hong Kong could broaden the range of investors and industries available to Central Asian companies, rather than concentrating funding in a single sector or source.

The discussion treated Hong Kong as a route into a wider international financial market, rather than as a single-source funding channel.

The panel sketched several routes to international capital: private funds, investment banks, AIX links with other financial centres and Hong Kong’s capital markets.

For venture investors such as Gobi, the story starts earlier, with founders who can build across borders.

For those founders, the appeal of the Astana-Hong Kong route is practical: access to investors who understand their businesses and can support their expansion. It connects the financing needs Mukazhanova described with the cross-border ambitions Tsao sees in the region’s entrepreneurs.

Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication.

At night, some of the most consequential robots in China are the ones nobody notices.

They move quietly through hotel corridors, wait for elevators, carry deliveries across campuses and clean underground car parks after most people have gone home. They do not walk like humans, hold conversations or perform on a stage. Their value lies somewhere less dramatic: they show up, complete a defined task and do it again the next day.

This is the world Excelland Robotics has been building in for more than a decade.

Founded in Shenzhen in 2013, Excelland started with robot control systems before moving into complete commercial service robots. Its machines now operate across hotels, offices, entertainment venues, campuses, shopping malls and transportation hubs. The company is preparing to list in Hong Kong under the name Excelland Robotics (Wuxi) Co. Ltd., but its story began long before the IPO—in a period when “commercial robotics” meant persuading businesses to trust machines with ordinary work.

The company’s prospectus describes a business that had sold more than 114,600 robots to over 5,100 customers globally as of March 2026. Behind that number is a particular approach to robotics: start with a narrow task, build a product around it and gradually expand the technology into more complicated environments.

The result is not one universal machine. It is a family of robots designed to make automation fit into the places where people already work.

The First Job Was Delivery

Excelland’s first major product was Yomie, an indoor delivery robot launched in 2016.

The timing mattered. Hotels and entertainment venues were looking for ways to handle repetitive service tasks while dealing with rising labour costs and high staff turnover. A delivery robot did not need to replace an entire employee. It needed to move an item from one point to another, reliably enough that staff could spend more time on work that required human attention.

Excelland followed Yomie with Yodee in 2017, a higher-capacity indoor delivery robot aimed at leisure and entertainment venues. It later introduced the Yogel line for on-demand delivery and campus applications.

By 2019, the company’s robot shipments had exceeded 2,500 units. In 2021, cumulative shipments passed 10,000. These were still small numbers compared with the mass-market hardware businesses that dominate China’s technology industry, but commercial robots operate under a different standard. Every deployment is also an operating environment, a source of data and a test of whether a product can survive outside the laboratory.

A robot that works once is a demonstration. A robot that works every day is a business.

That distinction has shaped Excelland’s development. Instead of betting everything on a single breakthrough product, the company has built a portfolio around specific jobs.

Yomie focuses on indoor delivery and guest guidance. Yodee is designed for larger-capacity indoor delivery. Yogel supports on-demand delivery. Yoxiaogu is built for cleaning, both indoors and outdoors. Yoshop is a family of vending robots for unmanned retail.

The names may be unfamiliar outside China, but the commercial logic is straightforward. Each product is designed around a setting where the task is repetitive, measurable and difficult to staff efficiently.

From Hotel Corridors to Harder Environments

Indoor delivery was only the beginning.

The company introduced indoor cleaning robots in 2022 and outdoor cleaning robots in 2023. That shift took Excelland into more demanding environments, where the robot could no longer depend on a predictable corridor or a controlled building layout.

An underground car park, for example, can be exposed to heat, exhaust fumes and vehicle traffic. Outdoor spaces introduce uneven surfaces, changing light, pedestrians and obstacles that may not exist the next time the robot passes through the same area.

These environments require more than a motor and a map. They require the machine to understand where it is, identify what is around it and make decisions as conditions change.

Excelland says its technology has evolved from systems built mainly around LiDAR and simultaneous localization and mapping to a multi-sensor architecture that combines cameras, LiDAR and other onboard sensors. Its robots use these systems to perceive obstacles, identify pathways, recognize facilities such as elevator panels and adjust their movements.

The company’s newest Yomie models show how small technical improvements can have commercial consequences.

The Yomie MX, launched in March 2026, is designed to complete multi-floor deliveries without requiring an elevator to be retrofitted with an Internet of Things system. Using visual recognition and an intelligent robotic arm, it can identify and press elevator buttons.

For a human, pressing an elevator button is barely an action. For a robot, it is a combination of perception, positioning, motion control and physical interaction. The machine must recognize the panel, move into the right position, operate the button and continue its route.

Commercial robotics is full of such apparently minor problems. The companies that solve them are often more valuable than the companies that merely produce the most impressive demonstration.

The Machine Is Only Half the Product

Excelland’s technology is spread across both the robot and the cloud.

The edge-side system handles real-time functions such as visual perception, positioning, navigation and motion control. The cloud side supports data management, model training, task coordination, remote management and ongoing optimization.

This cloud-edge architecture allows the company to reuse its underlying capabilities across different products. A perception system developed for delivery robots can contribute to cleaning or vending applications. Data from deployed machines can help refine algorithms and improve the performance of future products.

The same technology is also being commercialized outside robotics.

Through its Yoware platform, Excelland provides AI vision model solutions for industries including construction, building installation, sports, education, food production and media. These solutions can analyze images and video for functions such as object detection, scene recognition and anomaly detection.

That business changes the way Excelland should be understood. It is not only a robot manufacturer. It is also trying to become a provider of visual intelligence that can be deployed on cameras, edge computing devices and existing customer systems.

In 2025, the company generated RMB119.2 million from AI vision model solutions, representing 37.5% of total revenue. Robotic product sales contributed RMB135.0 million, while robots-as-a-service generated RMB49.9 million.

The numbers suggest that Excelland is gradually moving away from a simple hardware model. Its future may depend on whether it can turn the technology developed for physical robots into software, services and operating systems that customers continue to use.

Selling the Outcome, Not Just the Robot

The company is also experimenting with a different relationship with customers.

Under its robots-as-a-service model, Excelland retains ownership of the robot and deploys it at a customer site. Customers typically pay according to completed delivery orders or the amount of time a cleaning robot operates.

This approach is important because the upfront price of a robot is only one part of the adoption decision. A hotel operator or cleaning company is more interested in whether the machine can lower operating costs, reduce staffing pressure and deliver a predictable return.

A service model can make that decision easier. Customers pay for the work rather than simply purchasing the equipment. Excelland, meanwhile, remains involved in deployment, maintenance and operational support.

The model also creates a potential source of recurring revenue, although it comes with its own challenges. The company must manage its own fleet, keep machines working and absorb more of the operational risk.

Excelland’s revenue increased from RMB243.8 million in 2023 to RMB317.7 million in 2025. But it remained loss-making, reporting a net loss of RMB110.8 million in 2025 and RMB31.2 million in the first three months of 2026.

That is the less glamorous side of the robotics business. Building a fleet requires research, manufacturing, service infrastructure and customer acquisition before the benefits of scale fully appear.

Excelland’s five largest customers accounted for 76.4% of revenue in 2025, while its largest customer contributed 36.7%. The company also faces pricing pressure in hotel delivery robots, where competition has pushed down average selling prices.

The commercial question is therefore not simply whether Excelland can sell more robots. It is whether each deployment can become more efficient, more repeatable and more profitable.

A Cautious Bet on Embodied Intelligence

The language around robotics is changing quickly.

A few years ago, a company like Excelland would have been described mainly as a maker of service robots. Today, it is also talking about vision-language models, robotic arms, vision-language-action systems and embodied intelligence.

The shift reflects a wider ambition across the robotics industry: to build machines that can interpret their environments, understand instructions and perform more complex tasks.

But Excelland’s path is different from that of a humanoid robotics startup starting from a blank sheet of paper. The company already has robots operating in commercial environments, along with deployment data, customer relationships and experience integrating hardware with software.

That installed base could become an advantage if the company can use it to develop more capable systems. It could also become a constraint if the economics of existing products remain weak or if newer technologies require another long and expensive cycle of development.

For now, it is more accurate to say that Excelland is trying to use its commercial robotics platform as a foundation for embodied intelligence—rather than claiming that it has already become an embodied-intelligence company.

The distinction matters. Its current machines are still mostly specialized systems designed for defined tasks. Their strength is reliability within a particular environment, not general-purpose reasoning.

The Next Chapter Begins Outside China

Excelland plans to expand its products into selected overseas markets, including Thailand, Japan and South Korea. It has already shipped Yoxiaogu cleaning robots to South Korea and Yomie delivery robots to Japan, while exploring opportunities in Europe, North America, Malaysia and Singapore.

The opportunity is understandable. Hotels, campuses, shopping centres and cleaning operators around the world face many of the same labour and efficiency pressures. But international expansion will require more than translating a product manual. Robots must comply with local certifications, operate within unfamiliar buildings and meet different expectations around service, safety and maintenance.

That is where the Hong Kong listing enters the story.

Excelland is expected to begin trading under stock code 03231. The company says it plans to use the proceeds to expand research and development, strengthen sales and marketing, pursue strategic acquisitions and fund broader business expansion.

The IPO is therefore less a conclusion than a measure of confidence. Excelland is asking public-market investors to believe that the practical robots already working in hotels, offices and campuses can become the foundation of a larger technology platform.

The company’s future will not be decided by whether robots can produce a spectacular demo. It will be decided in the quiet moments: when a machine reaches the right floor, avoids the obstacle in its path, completes the task and returns to work the next day.

That may be the real test of commercial robotics—not whether a machine can look human, but whether it can become dependable enough to be part of the workplace.

Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

What does a humanoid robot boom actually look like? In China, it is taking shape not only in capital investment and production, but in the growing range of places where robots are being put to use.

Unitree helped put China’s robotics boom on the global radar, with quadruped and humanoid robots that drew attention through high-profile demos and commercial sales. In August 2026, Unitree listed on Shanghai’s STAR Market, with shares opening at RMB 1,100 — 629% above the RMB 150.80 offering price — and briefly valuing the company at RMB 444.9 billion. Two weeks later, the stock had fallen by more than half.

The correction, however, has not erased Unitree’s operating momentum. The company generated RMB 1.15 billion in first-half revenue, up 48.5% year over year, while cumulative production of its bipedal humanoid robots reached about 18,000 units.

Overseas investors are also increasing their exposure to China’s robotics sector. KraneShares’ KOID humanoid-robotics ETF holds Unitree alongside other Chinese robotics companies, while Defiance launched a U.S.-listed ETF focused on China’s humanoid robotics ecosystem.

Unitree’s rise captures one side of China’s robotics boom. Elsewhere, companies are writing very different chapters of the same story — tackling problems as specific as grasping an unfamiliar object, carrying hotel luggage, or handling repetitive work in a warehouse.

From Picking Things Up to Doing Real Work

For Hefei-based Zerith, useful robots start with an ordinary human action: picking something up. Founded in 2025 by members of Tsinghua University’s AI and robotics community, the startup’s wheeled H1 robot, priced at RMB 199,000 ($29,000), began global shipments in the second quarter of 2026. Its generalized-grasping systems are designed to handle varied objects and changing environments.

By January 2026, Zerith robots had already entered commercial settings, including Hefei Xinqiao International Airport; by April, they were also deployed at Olé supermarkets in Shenzhen and Hefei. In March 2026, three pilot robot stores opened in Shanghai, where the top-performing location recorded weekly sales above RMB 20,000 (about $3,000) during the May Day holiday. The company raised more than RMB 100 million in April 2026, by which point its orders had also exceeded RMB 100 million.

Beijing-based RobotEra is tackling manipulation from the hand outward. Founded in 2023 by Tsinghua assistant professor Chen Jianyu and Xi Yue, it develops five-finger dexterous hands alongside humanoid robots, with logistics as an early commercial target. The company’s robots are working with China Post and SF Express across more than 10 logistics centers, with orders exceeding RMB 500 million.

Capital has followed quickly. RobotEra raised RMB 1 billion (about $146 million) in March 2026 at a valuation above RMB 10 billion (about $1.46 billion), more than $200 million in another round led by SF Group, and RMB 1 billion in July led by Chengtong Fund.

Zerith and RobotEra illustrate how the boom is splintering into different commercial bets, but both face the same test: whether robots can perform everyday work reliably enough for customers to keep paying for them.

Making Robots Fit Into Human Spaces

The boom is also spreading beyond warehouses and industrial settings into services, where robots have to work around people rather than production lines.

At a Shangri-La hotel in Shanghai, eight Keenon robots handle greetings, luggage, room deliveries, cleaning and food service. The system reduced demand for repetitive labor by about 30%, improved service response efficiency by roughly 40%, and cut guest waiting times by about 35%.

Founded in Shanghai in 2010 by Li Tong, Keenon built its business around delivery robots before expanding into cleaning and humanoid systems. Its strategy is role-first: specialized robots handle standardized work, while humanoids take on tasks requiring more interaction and flexibility.

Keenon has shipped more than 100,000 robots, with products deployed across more than 70 countries and regions and over 600 cities, spanning restaurants, hotels, healthcare, retail and other service settings.

Keenon’s scale shows another side of China’s robotics boom: rather than waiting for a general-purpose humanoid to do everything, companies are already using narrower robot systems to test where automation can produce measurable value in everyday service work.

Shenzhen-based Digital Huaxia, founded in 2024, is testing another part of the service market: humanoids designed for more natural human interaction. Its approach combines facial expressions, voice interaction, emotion recognition and memory, but the company is focusing first on business and public-service settings rather than homes.

Its robots have been deployed or piloted in finance, government services, education and healthcare, including more than 20 ICBC branches. Digital Huaxia secured orders at the RMB 100 million level in its first year, with AgiBot participating in its angel financing.

Keenon and Digital Huaxia show how China’s robotics boom is moving into human-facing services, where the challenge is not only whether robots can perform useful tasks, but whether they can fit reliably into existing service workflows and deliver measurable value.

A Broader Robot Boom

China’s humanoid robot boom is broadening into a more diverse commercial ecosystem, as investment, production and deployment expand and companies pursue different products, business models and application scenarios. What is emerging is not a single path to commercialization, but a wider market taking shape across industrial and service settings.

Huawei unveiled the Kirin 9050 Pro on Monday at its HUAWEI Mate XT 2 product launch event. The release marks the company’s first new Kirin chip introduced at a flagship product launch in six years.

The chip makes its debut in the HUAWEI Mate XT 2 Ultimate, Huawei’s new tri-folding smartphone, with the company saying that overall device performance has improved by 42% compared with the previous-generation Mate XTs.

According to Huawei, the Kirin 9050 Pro uses a two-layer vertical stacking architecture based on its Tao Law technology framework. The design adds vertical interconnects inside the chip to shorten signal transmission paths.

Huawei says that, without relying on conventional geometric scaling in manufacturing equipment or process nodes, the chip increases transistor density from 155 MTr/mm² to 238 MTr/mm². Its performance cores reach a peak frequency of 3.1GHz, while the area used by its high-speed global on-chip network data paths is reduced by 55%. SRAM operating frequency has also increased by more than 40%, according to the company.

On the performance side, the Kirin 9050 Pro features Huawei’s Lingxi CPU hyperthreading technology. Huawei says its peak single-core performance is 24% higher than the previous generation, while multi-core performance has increased by 52%.

The chip also adds support for hardware-accelerated real-time ray tracing with up to 50 million calculations. It has been optimized for HarmonyOS 7 and works with Huawei’s Ark Engine. The company says the combination can extend overall battery life by an additional 36 minutes.

The HUAWEI Mate XT 2 Ultimate, the first device to feature the Kirin 9050 Pro, adopts a new wing-shaped G-type dual-inward-folding design. It has a 6.5-inch outer display and a 10.2-inch inner display when fully unfolded, while weighing 299 grams.

The phone also introduces a foldable Lingdun privacy display and a third-generation Red Maple camera system, along with video recording with an 18EV dynamic range. Huawei says its color reproduction has improved by 95% compared with the previous generation. The device packs a 5,600mAh battery and supports 50W wireless charging.

The HUAWEI Mate XT 2 Ultimate starts at RMB 19,999 ($2,980) and will go on sale on September 12. A dedicated bundle that includes a stylus will be available from September 23.

The Kirin 9050 Pro’s debut in the Mate XT 2 allows Huawei to further optimize the interaction between its chip architecture, operating system and hardware. Rather than simply focusing on higher chip specifications, this integration of hardware and software is particularly important for a tri-folding smartphone, as its larger display and more complex form factor place greater demands on performance scheduling, power efficiency, multitasking and app compatibility.

The combination of the Kirin 9050 Pro and HarmonyOS 7 in the Mate XT 2 can also be seen as another step in Huawei’s efforts to strengthen coordination between its chips, operating system and devices.

As the chip is introduced in more flagship devices, its real-world performance in everyday use, gaming, image processing and power efficiency will provide a clearer indication of the maturity of Huawei’s latest chip architecture.

With access to advanced manufacturing processes remaining a challenge, whether Huawei can continue to improve performance and power efficiency through architectural design, chip stacking and hardware-software optimization will also be closely watched.

Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

At a Sept. 1 online media briefing for the 23rd UBS Securities A-Share Seminar, discussion around China’s AI sector centered on a practical question: can lower costs and wider AI use translate into real business value?

UBS Securities China internet analyst Xiong Wei highlighted three themes to watch in China’s large-model sector: model capability, “token ROI” and monetization. While Chinese developers continue to improve their models — particularly in coding and agentic capabilities — companies using AI are becoming more selective about how much intelligence they actually need for a given task.

That marks a shift from “token-maxxing,” or encouraging more AI usage, toward “token optimization,” Xiong said. After rising AI bills made it harder for enterprises to measure the economic value generated by their token consumption, buyers have begun paying greater attention to the balance between performance and price. Xiong said that trend favors Chinese open-source models, whose improving capabilities and lower costs make them increasingly viable for repetitive or lower-risk workloads.

Xiong estimated that some leading Chinese models may cost less than one-tenth as much to develop as overseas peers, while average API pricing can be around 10% to 20% of international competitors. However, cheaper AI does not automatically translate into more revenue.

Kenneth Fong, UBS’s head of China internet research, said China’s major internet platforms face a more fundamental constraint: user traffic and time spent on mobile devices are no longer growing much. AI can lower content-production costs and make advertising or recommendation systems more effective, but consumers still have limited time and attention. He used AI-generated short dramas as an example: producing more shows at lower cost does not mean they will capture more of viewers’ time and attention.

A new experiment from Mango TV illustrates both sides of that equation. The Later Journey to the West, an AIGC-produced fantasy series, debuted on Mango TV and in Hunan Satellite TV’s prime-time slot on Aug. 31, becoming China’s first AIGC long-form series to reach a satellite-TV prime-time slot.

Adapted from an anonymously written late-Ming or early-Qing fantasy novel of the same name, the story follows a new generation of characters who reunite for another journey to obtain Buddhist scriptures after the originals are misunderstood.

Its first season is planned to run for 30 episodes of about 40 minutes each. The series is being made with Mango Lingchuang, Mango TV’s in-house AIGC production platform, which had served more than 40,000 professional users and supported over 3,900 projects by mid-2026.

The platform generated 109 character assets and 143 scene assets for the series, while the project is also testing a “produce, review and broadcast in parallel” model, allowing later episodes to remain in production as earlier ones air. The series also showed some early audience traction: real-time ratings for its Aug. 31 premiere ranked first among provincial satellite channels in the same time slot, according to ITHome, while ChinaTimes reported that it had logged 27.57 million plays on Mango TV by Sept. 2.

Yet whether those efficiencies and early audience gains can translate into a sustainable business remains unclear. Before the series aired, Hunan’s broadcasting regulator asked the project team to explore both a workable technical path for AI-powered long-form storytelling and a commercialization path for AIGC seasonal dramas.

That challenge echoes points made by both Xiong and Fong: as AI becomes cheaper to use and lowers production costs, the focus is shifting from how much AI can produce to whether its use can generate sufficient economic value.

In September, China’s first dedicated departmental regulation for micro-dramas, the Administrative Measures for the Development of Micro-Dramas, officially took effect, bringing AI-generated micro-dramas under a tiered regulatory framework for the first time.

The move marks more than just the beginning of a new era of compliance. It signals that China’s AI short drama industry is moving beyond its early, anything-goes phase of chasing traffic through sheer production volume and entering a new cycle driven by both technology and content.

The regulation, which came into effect on September 1, places all micro-dramas with individual episodes shorter than 20 minutes under a unified national regulatory framework. It also requires AI-generated micro-dramas to carry prominent AI disclosure labels in every episode.

Streaming platforms are prohibited from using recommendation algorithms designed to encourage excessive consumption or user addiction. By assigning responsibilities across the entire production, review, and distribution process, the rules are pushing the industry away from unchecked growth and toward a healthier ecosystem built around quality and responsible innovation.

Looking back at the explosive growth of the past two years, the first wave of AI short dramas was built largely on the technological dividend of lower costs and higher efficiency. Rapid advances in generative AI have compressed the production costs of short dramas, which could easily run into hundreds of thousands of yuan using traditional methods, to just a few thousand yuan. Projects that once required a crew of more than a dozen people and months of production can now be completed by a single creator using AI tools in just a few weeks.

In the first half of 2026, the industry released 367,000 micro-dramas, with AI-generated productions accounting for more than 74%. More than 1,500 new AI dramas entered the market every day on average, turning the once-theoretical concept of a “one-person production team” into a practical reality for countless small and independent creators.

But the side effects of this rapid, volume-driven growth soon became apparent. Platforms were flooded with interchangeable AI-generated faces and recycled storylines, while the industry-wide rate of recouping production costs remained low.

The resulting bubble of low-quality content threatened to push the entire sector into a vicious cycle where inferior productions crowded out higher-quality work.

The turning point came with the systematic technological upgrades undertaken by leading platforms. Rather than simply opening AI production tools to everyone without restrictions, major players such as ByteDance’s Hongguo Short Drama began building full-stack AI production systems specifically designed for short dramas.

These platforms have fine-tuned large language models specifically for short drama production. They have also used billions of user behavior signals to develop tools that optimize script pacing and reduce low-quality and recycled content at the source.

Platforms are also moving to address some of the technical bottlenecks that have long plagued AI short dramas. Character consistency technology is helping tackle the problem of characters changing appearance across episodes, while multimodal video models are being optimized for the short shots and fast-paced storytelling typical of micro-dramas.

Platforms have also introduced AI content pre-screening systems that can flag issues such as repeated AI-generated faces, potentially infringing materials, and visual defects before a production enters the formal review process.

These efforts point to a broader shift in the industry. AI is no longer being used simply to maximize production volume. Instead, platforms are increasingly applying technology to improve consistency, quality, and compliance throughout the production pipeline. The result is a gradual move away from low-cost mass production toward a more quality-driven model of AI short drama production.

At the same time, a second growth curve for AI short dramas is emerging overseas. From January to July 2026, TikTok short dramas generated more than $110 million in cumulative revenue-sharing payouts, with monthly payouts exceeding $29 million in July alone.

The AI production technologies and highly engaging storytelling formulas refined in China are now being rapidly replicated in global markets, making AI short dramas a new benchmark for China’s digital content exports.

Looking back from this new starting point, AI short dramas were never meant to replace film and television with AI. Their real role is to empower creators by using technology to reshape the economics and relationships of content production.

As low-quality, mass-produced, and recycled content is squeezed out by both regulation and technological advances, the core competitive advantage that will endure is not simply the AI tools themselves, but creators’ ability to accurately capture audience emotions and control narrative pacing.

More value across the AI short drama supply chain is likely to concentrate around leading players with strong IP libraries, foundational AI capabilities, and global distribution networks. China’s experiment with industrializing AI-powered content production has only just entered the stage with the greatest room for imagination.

Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

A robot cooked noodles in about a minute. Another prepared breakfast. Humanoids climbed stairs, crawled across obstacles and sparred inside a fighting cage. Elsewhere, robots sorted packages, fetched medicine and practiced jobs ranging from household chores to emergency rescue.

The scenes at the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC), held from Aug. 19 to 23 in Beijing, offered a glimpse of an industry trying to answer a bigger question: how can increasingly capable machines fit into the way people live and work?

Under the theme “Human-Robot Symbiosis, Production-Demand Convergence,” the five-day event brought together hundreds of robotics companies and thousands of products. Some 373 companies showcased more than 3,000 products, including 311 debuts, alongside dozens of new technologies and solutions.

Robots get busy — and sometimes creative

On the exhibition floor, the emphasis was not only on what robots could perform, but where they could be useful.

Galaxea AI presented several new models, including the Galbot ET1, G1, and S1. In a simulated home setting, the G1 made breakfast by toasting bread and pouring drinks. When the cup was moved mid-pour, the robot returned the pitcher upright to avoid spilling, relocated the cup, and resumed pouring.

CASBOT brought a different kind of performance to the show floor: a robot rock band complete with an electric guitarist, bassist, keyboard player and drummer.

The four-machine ensemble played Chinese rock favorites, including Beyond’s “Glorious Years” and “Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies,” before performing an original track titled “Heat Dissipation.”

Li-Gong demonstrated two LiDian F1 robots working together in a continuous industrial workflow, disassembling parts, sorting and transporting them, then reassembling and returning them — a showcase of how embodied intelligence could be applied to factory operations.

Unitree’s robots also stepped into the ring for kickboxing matches. In the 40-kilogram final, a team from North China Electric Power University remotely controlled a Unitree G1 to defeat another G1 operated by Unitree’s own team, taking the championship — a result Beijing Daily summed up with the playful headline: “defeat”

The show floor also featured a growing number of biomimetic robots from companies including UBTECH, AheadForm, Noetix Robotics and HokMind. Their designs are becoming increasingly humanlike, with developers refining everything from body proportions and joint movement to facial expressions, skin and hair.

Some of the most memorable moments, however, came when robots behaved in unexpected ways.

At the World Humanoid Robot Games held in Beijing during the same week, the 1.35-meter-tall Tiangong Omni won the small-size 400-meter race in 45.66 seconds. But its running style attracted almost as much attention as its speed: the robot leaned forward with its arms raised close to its face, prompting Chinese internet users to compare it to someone shyly “covering its face” while running.

Its developers had not originally designed the pose. Han Gang, a motion-control algorithm expert at the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, said developed Han said rapid arm swinging could place greater loads on the shoulder joints, increasing heat and energy consumption over the 400-meter race.

Beyond the demonstration

China’s humanoid robot boom is entering a critical test: moving from stage demonstrations and “small-batch trials” to reliable, large-scale use. identified, and said.

Most of the time, when we talk about embodied intelligence, the first things that come to mind are factories, warehouses, and robots doing actual work. Qianxing Intelligence, however, is taking a different route: instead of spending too much time talking about the future in the lab, it is putting robots straight into entertainment venues. And not the kind of robots you simply stand around and watch.

Its flagship product, Iron Armor Battle Arena, essentially turns mech combat into something people can actually play in the real world. Think about a traditional arcade: screens, joysticks, a few buttons, and players sitting in front of a machine, furiously mashing controls. Qianxing Intelligence flips that model around.

Players use motion-sensing controllers to operate actual humanoid boxing robots on a dedicated arena. Punches, dodges, blocks, and combos are all mapped from the player’s movements to the physical robot in real time.

What used to be playing a fighting game becomes actually fighting with a robot.

The real challenge here isn’t how cool the robot looks. It’s the sense of control. What matters is how much delay there is between a punch and the robot’s movement, whether the force feedback feels convincing, and whether the robot responds naturally enough to feel like an extension of the player.

Those details can make the difference between something that merely looks impressive and something people genuinely want to play. Qianxing Intelligence said it has fine-tuned the system to enable millisecond-level synchronization between the player and the robot.

The company doesn’t make each match particularly long. A typical battle lasts around one to two minutes, with both real-time two-player matches and single-player challenge modes available. For arcades, shopping malls, and theme parks, that design is actually pretty practical: players get a quick, intense experience, while operators get faster turnover. The current replay rate is around 40% to 50%, according to the company.

Qianxing Intelligence also has designed the product with the business needs of venue operators in mind from the beginning. Take the mech’s modular exterior. The outer shell can be swapped relatively easily. One day, it can be a standard mech. The next, it can carry a branded collaboration skin. During a holiday event, the same machine can take on an entirely different theme.

The robot’s voice can be customized. The system comes with an AI-powered voice interaction layer that can handle match commentary and gameplay prompts, while also supporting customized personalities and scripted content.

For theme parks, shopping malls, and tourism projects, this opens up an interesting possibility: the robot doesn’t have to remain just a piece of equipment. It can become part of the venue’s IP.

On the business side, Qianxing Intelligence is currently pursuing a fairly straightforward two-track model. On one side, it works with arcade chains, shopping malls, and theme parks to deploy machines through revenue-sharing or rental arrangements. On the other, it sells complete systems to operators in overseas markets, while generating longer-term revenue through consumables, content updates, and customized IP skins.

The interesting part is that the company isn’t really selling just a robot. Selling the hardware is only the first step. There is content, IP, operations, and ongoing services layered on top. That model is also helping the product move beyond China. It has entered markets including Malaysia, the US, and the UK, with overseas customers accounting for close to half of its client base, according to Qianxing Intelligence.

That international focus also explains why the company has paid attention to global safety and quality standards from the outset. A location-based entertainment robot is very different from a lab prototype. Once you put it into commercial venues across different countries, safety, reliability, and maintenance costs all become very real questions.

If that were the end of the story, Qianxing Intelligence would simply be a company that figured out how to turn robots into a pretty cool arcade attraction. But the more interesting question is what comes next. What if mech combat is only the first game?

Cross-venue rankings, mech leagues, collaborations with major IPs, online-offline competitions and social gameplay—all of these could eventually turn Iron Armor Battle Arena from a single entertainment machine into a broader competitive and social platform built around physical robots.

And that may be the most interesting thing about Qianxing Intelligence. It isn’t trying to sell embodied intelligence as some distant, futuristic concept that ordinary people can barely relate to. Its approach is much simpler and arguably much more effective: let people play with it first.

After all, telling people that the era of embodied intelligence has arrived probably doesn’t mean much to most of us.

But if one day you walk into a shopping mall, scan a QR code, pick up a controller, and start throwing punches through a real robot against your friend, that might be the moment when embodied intelligence actually starts to feel like part of everyday life.

Gamescom 2026 is being held in Cologne, Germany, from August 26 to 30. During Opening Night Live, miHoYo unveiled its new original IP NODUSFALL for the first time and released its world premiere trailer, which showcased glimpses of the game’s combat mechanics and world setting.

Compared with the anime-style characters and RPG-focused gameplay seen in many of miHoYo’s previous titles, the new game takes a noticeably different approach in both visual style and combat design.

Based on the footage shown at the event, NODUSFALL is being developed with Unreal Engine 5, with the demo focusing on exploration, combat and multiplayer cooperation. Players can control customizable characters as they explore ruins suspended above a sea of clouds.

Floating platforms, structures and other elements of the environment can change in response to player actions and attacks from giant creatures, with physics-based effects adding a greater sense of spatial interaction to combat.

Multiplayer co-op is one of the key features showcased in the demo. The game introduces a combat system built around Elemental Links, where players can create different energy nodes on giant elemental creatures through various weapons and attacks, then coordinate with other players to exploit them.

The demo showed support for teams of up to four players, while characters can also make use of environmental mechanisms during battles, such as using floating platforms to quickly reach a creature and target specific parts of its body.

Rather than relying primarily on character skills to deal damage, this design places greater emphasis on coordination between players and the role of the environment in combat. The scale and attack patterns of the giant creatures also give the battles a distinct hunting-game feel, setting NODUSFALL apart from miHoYo’s previous open-world and action RPG titles.

The demo also offered a closer look at the game’s world for the first time. The story takes place across floating continents formed after the shattering of the Source Core.

The scattered Elements have transformed the local ecosystem and granted different powers to certain creatures and humans. Players take on the role of Linkers and explore various ruins as they gradually uncover the reasons that led to the destruction of the Source Core.

Based on what has been revealed so far, NODUSFALL does not follow the traditional anime-style RPG formula seen in titles such as Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail. It puts greater focus on a more realistic fantasy world, action-oriented combat and multiplayer co-op.

More details about the characters, regions and business model of NODUSFALL have yet to be revealed, and miHoYo has not announced an official release date. According to miHoYo, the development of NODUSFALL has been underway for more than four years.

For miHoYo, which has already established a strong lineup of anime-style games, the new title marks an attempt to explore a different genre and potentially reach a different segment of the global gaming market.

Whether this approach can attract players in an increasingly competitive global gaming market will depend on how miHoYo further develops the game’s content and long-term operations.
